utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd reached paragraphs 19 and 20 of the summary. On the atlas Exhibit 336, page 37. Bileca referred to in paragraph 19, the last sentence, can be found in square E-2, immediately north of the lake border and thus north and slightly east of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hausvicka, I think you either told us or were just about to tell us that, following your confession or the account that you've given, the officers, the JNA officers, told you that if you'd said that before, you wouldn't be beaten, and you were then taken to Bileca barracks.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On arrival at those barracks on the 22nd of October, were you confined on a solitary basis? Were you tied to a bed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when soldiers, JNA soldiers there, passed by you? What did they do to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they brought me into that room or solitary confinement cell, they tied my legs to the lower half of the bed and my arms to the upper half of the bed. I don't know how long the guards beat me and took turns in beating me on all parts of my body. As I was tied, I wasn't able to defend myself, and they beat me all over my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was on a regular, daily basis for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the first month of these beatings, were you taken for interrogation by a Sergeant or Master Sergeant Stevic, who is a Serbian security officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact know this man yourself from earlier days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him from the JNA, the army, when I did my military service on Mount Kopaonik. I think there was a ceremony to mark Security Day that the army observed. I didn't meet him personally, but I saw him there. He was there among the other officers who were attending the ceremony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what corps was he a member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was Security Day, I think he belonged to that branch of the Armed Services, security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did he interrogate you and, just in a sentence or so because I don't want you to go more than necessary into this distressing experience, in a sentence or so, how were you treated at interrogation by him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He interrogated me on several occasions, was very brutal and violent towards me, which meant that he beat me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did such interrogations generally end and where did they end?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the interrogations, I would be taken off to a toilet where the guard would beat me up, and then at the next interrogation, the Staff Sergeant Stevic asked me, "Are you smarter now, and will you be able to give us smarter answers now?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That toilet to which you were taken, did you notice anything about it and see any traces of something there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were traces of blood. There were traces of blood, including my own blood, but I already found bloodstains there from previous prisoners, I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of Yugoslavia did Stevic come from? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- I think he was from the environs of Uzice because he belonged to the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While detained, were you also obliged to work under conditions of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of tasks did you do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to saw wood, and we had to load up trucks with various furniture items, electrical goods, probably stolen goods that had been looted from around Dubrovnik. We had to wash cars that had Dubrovnik number plates on them, trucks, buses, passenger vehicles and so on, and some officers even drove cars of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of forced labour, what methods of punishment or enforcement were used on you and other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that kind of labour, we would be exposed to swear words, they would spit at us, and let me just give you an illustration: We were carrying something that was 200 kilos in weight, and we had to carry it up to the third floor - a safe of some kind - and the military policemen beat us with electric batons, and they would beat us on the head and the lower parts of our body, and it's very difficult for me to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take no further details from you, but just because the Judges may not be familiar with this particular item, an electric baton, is that something that releases an electric shock into the person by whom it is touched?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, you don't beat with that kind of baton but it has two wires at the top of it, and when you press somebody's body with it, it causes an electric shock, especially if placed on the head or the lower extremities. Then they cause a great deal of pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many detainees at Bileca? What was the percentage of civilians and combatants and what were the ages of the people, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bileca, what I saw and what I know is that there were about 200 detainees. Civilians and fighters, the ratio was, say, 80 to 20 per cent. And their ages, the ages of the detainees or, rather, those civilians who were there was between 50 to 89, 90 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were combatants and civilians treated similarly or differently by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were treated the same. For them, we were all Ustashas and throat-cutters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The civilians, were they beaten, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can, if asked, give accounts of what you were told by others of the particularly savage and humiliating beatings that they received. If asked.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross, visit the prison while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the Judges, if you will, please, an account of what was done before those visits and what was done in the course of them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the first visits came, I was hidden away from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, when they registered me with the ICRC, the interpreters were mostly from Belgrade, and we didn't have any confidence and trust in them. We didn't think that they would do their job properly and translate properly to the International Red Cross representatives, so once the Red Cross had arrived, when she would do the interpreting, the prisoners would be beaten badly. And one of the detainees knew three languages very well; we'd do our own translating, so the representative of the Red Cross was astounded when we told her our story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beatings that occurred, did these occur after the ICRC visits and in respect of what had been said to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure of that, but we assumed so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to food and other aid packages provided by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received a package while the Red Cross was there, and they would spend an hour with us, what we managed to swallow and eat during that time that they were there, well and good. All the rest would be taken away once they'd left, by the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a United States citizen by the name of Marin Pesa detained? Was he revealed to the ICRC or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. My mistake. The question: Was he hidden first and subsequently revealed to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like me. He was hidden first, and when the International Red Cross turned up, we secretly managed to tell them that he was there too, so they looked for him and then he was revealed to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In November 1991, did you sign a form of confession? If so, explain how that came about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after those intensive interrogations, one day they brought a book in with about 50 pages, to sign and to say that that was my confession. I didn't have an opportunity to read through it all, and I just signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in any sense a voluntary document of yours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that as a result of that document, or for other reasons, you were going to be tried for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the officers themselves but the guards. They beat me because they read in the document that I had killed and slaughtered Serb children in Dubrovnik and that I had extracted their eyes and cut off their ears and did things like that in the Mokosica region. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of which was made up and you were forced to sign; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any of the prisoners there, to your knowledge, ever taken for trial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: January 1992, was there a short-lived change of management at the Bileca camp when the Uzice Corps changed to the Rijeka Corps, and the new commander, a man called Raseta, treated detainees more appropriately?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some ten days later, was there somebody called Captain Biga who features?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Biga was there in the camp all the time throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he then feature ten days after Raseta took over? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when this man Raseta came, he behaved quite differently towards us. So it was easier to live in the camp. But I suppose that when they learnt that he was doing some tasks that he had to do and that our conditions were slightly better at that time, they replaced him with a man called Ljubisic, Sergeant Ljubisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did conditions return to what they had before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps they were even worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In mid-April 1992 or thereabouts, were you moved with a group of about 70 prisoners to Morinje camp, which we can see on Exhibit 337, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that map is being produced, remind the learned Judges of its location. What were the conditions like in Morinje camp? Better, worse, or about the same as before?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can make mine available, if it helps. It doesn't matter. It's marked. It's probably more convenient that it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conditions were worse than in the Bileca camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Morinje, as we can see and as the Judges will have in mind, lies in Montenegro on one of the parts of Boka Kotorska, on the western edge of it. It's marked in blue. Conditions were worse. In what way were they worse?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a room. It might have been 50 or 60 square metres in size. It was a warehouse of some kind. The floor was a wooden floor. We had to lie on the floor, and we just had a bucket in which to urinate, and if we wanted to defecate, we would have to go outside and be beaten. So we didn't go outside, and we defecated in the bucket in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 28. I think you were subjected to various indignities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to ask this witness to relive the distressing experiences himself. There were mock executions, forced boxing matches, singing of Serbian nationalist songs, and any mistake in such things as the use of a guard's name would be sanctioned by a beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When guards came into the room, did you all have to jump to your feet and then look at your own feet?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That also could lead to arbitrary beatings by the guards?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The percentage of civilians to combatant detainees at this camp was similar to or different from that at Bileca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ratio was more or less the same, but for them we were all Ustashas and cut-throats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there a significant number of elderly men there from Croatia or from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that same Master Sergeant Ljubisic who had been at Morinje -- at Bileca also at the Morinje camp?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He would come on several occasions with guards from Bileca who came there to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the transfer of detainees between these two camps to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- well, actually, I can tell you my experience with those transfers. We were boarded up onto a bus. We had to sit three per seat, and if there wasn't any room for sitting down, you had to kneel. Three or four guards got into the bus. The journey lasted about two hours. They jumped on us, ran about, bit us, hit us, spat on us until we reached Morinje. When we got to the camp, I didn't know I actually had arrived in a camp, but from the road to the barracks where we were set up, there were about 300 metres and we had to run the gauntlet. There were soldiers on both sides with different objects in their hands. They had rifles, shovels, and things like that and we had to run the gauntlet for those 300 metres. They would beat us, we fell down, helped each other up, until we got to this shed. So we were really beaten up badly by the time we got to the shed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards and soldiers who beat you at the various locations you've described, what ethnicity or what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you exchanged on the 2nd of July in Cavtat? Did you join the exchange as a prisoner? Did you rejoin the Croatian Special Police Unit, leaving in mid-1994 for reasons that you've set out in your summary?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other matter of detail that I ought to have covered: Going right back to Mokosica and the killings at the shelter. If I haven't asked you this before, on that day, how were you dressed? Were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men from your unit were there in the shelter at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there. I was a hundred metres away from the shelter. But when I got there, I found them all standing in front of the shelter, picking up what was left of those people. So that I can't confirm whether they were actually in the shelter or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how many combatants altogether were there in that shelter, roughly, at the time that you were using it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exactly five of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask of this witness. I would invite the Chamber to have in mind during cross-examination that any cross-examination about the experiences that he suffered should have a specific and valid forensic purpose before it's permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me understand that. That he's not to be asked questions about his sufferings? Of course the Trial Chamber has in mind the sensitivity involved in this, but I'm not sure what else you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I have in mind. I mean, I think this is a witness who suffered gravely in the way he described, and the consequences for him in giving evidence are perhaps obvious, but I respectfully invite you to have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you hear the point that is made, that this is a witness who has suffered, and I'm sure you have in mind the need to deal sensitively with any cross-examination. Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hausvicka, you're testifying about the year 1991. All the events that took place were in that year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the beginning of 1992. In all those events, do you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any idea what the events in the vicinity of Dubrovnik have to do with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you assume that those events in the surroundings of Dubrovnik have anything to do with Serbia? What is the connection between those events and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I lived through, the JNA, with Serbia, attacked Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you're saying the JNA, with Serbia, attacked Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I correct my answer: The JNA with Serbian volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those Serbian volunteers, were they from Serbia or perhaps from some other republic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal experience tells me that they were mostly from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among Serbian volunteers from Serbia, who did you specifically see in Dubrovnik or its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in captivity in Bileca, I was questioned by the guards and the officers, and they were all from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they soldiers, officers, non-commissioned officers of the JNA, or members of some sort of formation from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were officers and reservists of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1991, the year you're testifying about, the SFRY still existed as a state, that the Yugoslav People's Army was in existence as the armed force of that state, that it was not subordinated to any single republic but, rather, to the federal state. It was the Yugoslav People's Army and that you were in conflict with the JNA in the area of Dubrovnik. Serbia is quite a long way from you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia and Montenegro border with Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know geography well, so let's not go into that. But let us look into these events a little. There are documents to show that as early as January 1991, there were illegal supplies of armaments arriving at Dubrovnik airport.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but as far as I know, there were no weapons in Dubrovnik, not even in September and October of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that for a whole decade there were no military forces in Dubrovnik because it is a tourist resort, that the closest garrison was the Trebinje garrison which is in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that, but I have to point out that there were no soldiers in October 1991 either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, who was it that was opening fire from the area of Dubrovnik on members of the JNA along the border with Montenegro and further up towards Ivanjica, which is also in the territory of Herzegovina? It's not even in the territory of Croatia. Who was it that was opening fire, and who was it that killed so many JNA soldiers in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I am not qualified to answer that question, but as far as I know, it was the other way round. It wasn't fire being opened from the Croatian side but from Ivanjica and the area of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recollect that the first soldiers killed were those on the border with Montenegro within the territory of Montenegro, then in Ravno in the territory of Herzegovina, that commemorations were held in Montenegro at the time because of those killings, and that 161 soldiers were killed in those events, 161 soldiers from Montenegro. Who killed those people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're wrong. I think that what you're talking about, 161 soldiers, I think this happened much later, when the most intensive attacks were launched against Dubrovnik. I was in captivity at the time and I'm not qualified to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But before you were captured, a moment ago Mr. Nice asked you whether you were wearing a uniform when you were captured. He didn't ask you whether you were carrying a weapon. You were carrying a weapon, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was captured? I was in uniform and I was carrying a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was what I had assumed. So you were in uniform and you were carrying a weapon when you were captured.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I was a member of the special police at the time, in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up to the events that you're testifying about before you were captured, in which combat operations did you take part against the JNA in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat operations against JNA were not possible in that area because we were shelled on a daily basis by the JNA. So not a single shell was fired in the direction of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that until you were captured, no one opened fire from Dubrovnik on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying regarding my area. But I am not qualified to say what happened in other areas because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that the army, over radio Herceg-Novi, which is very well-received in Dubrovnik, kept repeating the message not to open fire on the army and that not a single bullet would be fired if there is no fire against the JNA? It launched these appeals for fire not to be opened against the JNA. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right, because you can't receive Herceg-Novi in Dubrovnik. And secondly, I don't know about such appeals, and I think that nobody fired at the army, and the army did what it did in every village that it entered, from Konavle to Primorje. Either 50 per cent of the villages were burnt down or they were entirely burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you claiming that, without any cause or provocation, the army went around, opening fire on civilian buildings, that nobody opened fire at the army, and that nothing was happening against the army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, yes. There may have been instances of certain frontal clashes, but as far as I know, in the area in which I was, the army was free to walk through any village. No resistance was put up, and whichever village they entered in my part was burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, it is well known that the army entered Cavtat and that Cavtat remained completely intact. Wasn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By then I was already detained, so I don't know. I do know that the village of Zvekovica, just above Cavtat, was burned to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there any fighting there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you're talking about 1991 and the beginning of 1992, that was the period while Croatia was still not internationally recognised, is it true to say that the JNA had every right to be in the territory of Yugoslavia, which means Croatia as well as part of Yugoslavia, and that that was its constitutional obligation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that by then, there was already a referendum on the secession of Yugoslavia, and I think that the army had no need to be there. You said yourself that Dubrovnik was a tourist resort. And I think that Dubrovnik was not ready for all this, because we believed that our neighbours were clever enough and that they would never contemplate attacking such a pearl as Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can see from my documents, there was an order not to capture Dubrovnik, and Dubrovnik never was captured, as you know well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, Dubrovnik was defended. Had it been captured, I don't know what would have happened. But on the 6th of December, it was saved. But as for that order, I was detained, and I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was Dubrovnik defended?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying what I heard. About 20 brave men of Dubrovnik defended Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that the army attacked Dubrovnik, but some 20 brave men managed to defend it? Is that your story?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My story is that 20 men were forced to defend Dubrovnik from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So the army criminally attacked Dubrovnik in the aim of capturing it but it didn't succeed in doing so because it was defended by 20 brave men. Is that your story?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. A moment ago when Mr. Nice asked you what ethnicity JNA members were, you said that they were Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to establish that they were Serbs and Montenegrins? Did you ask them? Did they tell you that? On what basis did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said that most of them were Serbs and Montenegrins, because we didn't even know the names of some of the guards. But we knew some names, and the names of those we knew were mostly Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the JNA was composed of representatives of all nationalities of the former SFRY? Even in those days, even then when Croatia proclaimed its independence, there were still Croats in the JNA, not to say how many Macedonians there were, how many Hungarians, Albanians, Romanians, Ruthenians and other ethnicities. Do you know that the JNA consisted of representatives of all ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that, but when I was captured, the guards who beat us and who did what they did to us, those who introduced themselves were mostly Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, you said that when you were arrested, a man asked you whether you knew him. Is that right? And first of all, you didn't recognise him, and then later on you did recognise him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a beard. And I was badly beaten up, so I wasn't all there. And when he asked me whether I knew him, I couldn't recognise him straight away, but a minute or two later, I recollected and I said, "Yes, I know. You're Pero Miljevic," and he said, "Yes, I am Pero Miljevic," and I knew him personally from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't quite hear you well, what you said at the end. So he's a man from Dubrovnik, is he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he wore a beard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that no one in the JNA wears a beard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did serve in the JNA so that I do know that you have to be freshly shaved every morning, clean-shaven, but he had a JNA uniform on, so I assumed he was a JNA reservist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there other men there who were locals? You just said that he came from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other men I knew. Some of them not by name. Some were from Dubrovnik, some from Trebinje, some from Bileca, but in any event, they were all wearing JNA uniforms, and my acquaintance with them developed in the Trebinje barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that in the former SFRY, most of the reservists who had a military assignment kept a uniform at home so that when they were called up, they could put them on and report to wherever they were assigned to. Do you know that most of them had such uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. And when they called -- they were called up, they probably put them on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this the JNA or was it a paramilitary formation that happened to be near Dubrovnik? Because the JNA, when it called up reservists, it didn't form any local units. You served in the JNA, so you know that. For instance, as far as I understand, you did your military service somewhere in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Sombor and Kopaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I, for instance, did my military service in Zadar. So you from Croatia served in Serbia, and me from Serbia, I served in Croatia, in Zadar. Quite a long way away, actually. So in your opinion, was this a regular JNA unit or a paramilitary unit? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't understand these military formations. In my view, they were JNA reservists. They were all wearing JNA uniforms and insignia, and they were in the barracks, because if they hadn't been members, they couldn't have been in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the JNA, as it was placing under control certain parts of the territory where conflicts had broken out, Mostar, Capljina, Stolac, and then also in the area around Slano, which it placed under its control as it did Cavtat and so on, that not a single of these towns was destroyed or damaged while the JNA was there but that all those places were damaged later on in conflicts when the JNA withdrew from those areas. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer with respect to one particular place, because I didn't go to Mostar, Stolac, and Capljina for a long time, so I can't say. But when the JNA entered Slano, I was still not captured and fire was being set to buildings in Slano and it was burned down entirely. I can tell you that the same applies to Osojnik and some other places. Cavtat fared a little better, I don't know why, but all the other places surrounding Dubrovnik were more or less burnt to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you claiming that the JNA was not exposed in the area to strong activity by paramilitary units of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I'm claiming for that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in that period of time where you say there were no formations, and not only in that period time but even earlier, that throughout Croatia, JNA barracks were blocked, electricity and water supplies cut off, fire was opened at the barracks, soldiers and officers killed. Do you know how many soldiers and officers were killed in those blocked barracks who hadn't even left their barracks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know I know from the media, from the radio and television. As far as I know, in the barracks that were blocked, the troops were asked to withdraw. And whenever the officers agreed to do that, they were allowed to go home unscathed. That is as far as I can remember, but I personally was not present in any of those barracks to be able to claim either way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about what was happening all over Croatia as a result of the attacks of paramilitary formations on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything specifically, but as far as I know about paramilitary forces in Croatia, I think there's no need to talk about such forces because they never existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have some information here. I don't know whether you're familiar with it. And let me check it out with you, whether it is correct. At the very beginning of those operations, in a locality called Krivi Do - you're familiar with it, in Dubrovnik? - a military conscript from Niksic who was under the influence of alcohol and who had just learnt that his brother had died, had been killed, that he killed some innocent civilians, mostly elderly people, and he was convicted to a 20-year prison term. As you know, that is the maximum sentence according to the Yugoslav law that was in force. Rather, 15 is the maximum, and 20 replaces the death sentence. And his appeal was rejected, and he's still serving his sentence. So, for instance, this is a case that I have documented here. Are you aware of such an event?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really haven't heard of a location called Krivi Do, and I really don't know anything about that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, then, do you know and is it true that the JNA opened fire only on those buildings from which fire was opened at units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you specifically about the area where I was. There was no system in the shooting. Warehouses were fired at, civilian facilities, churches. There was simply no order in the firing. There was just firing, shooting, and destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described the killing of people by a shell where a police car was standing nearby, are you claiming that you, the police and those armed forces that you had in Dubrovnik, that as far as you know, at least, they never opened fire on the army? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it? Could you be a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you captured, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Up to the 21st of October, then, did you do any shooting, you personally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who shot then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the region I was in, nobody shot at the positions of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me how many armed persons were in Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would estimate that there were about a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that they shot from mortars, anti-aircraft guns, and other artillery pieces at the JNA at that time? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, but let me be specific and concrete. For the area I was in, there was quite certainly no shooting from any type of weapon. The JNA positions were not shot at at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you mean to say that you don't know that the JNA was shot at from Dubrovnik from cannons and mortars?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, no, there was no shooting from mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Do you happen to know that after the arrival of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the peace forces into the protected safe area in Croatia, that the situation in that part became highly complex and that additional reinforcements, Croatian reinforcements, to the tune of 8.000 men, were sent into the region? That is to say when the general conditions were being stabilised, because there was constant provocations and losses and casualties on the side of the JNA, although they were very reticent. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And don't you think that the whole situation around Dubrovnik had as its main task to paint a media picture and be used by the media first and foremost to promote this image against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the JNA painted its own picture by its acts, what it did in Dubrovnik and its environs. It burnt the environs and damaged a great deal of Dubrovnik. I think that that is sufficient -- a sufficient picture painted by the JNA to show the world how it stood and where it stood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true, do you know, that on the basis of an agreement that was reached by the President of the FRY at the time and Croatia, Dobrica Cosic and Dr. Tudjman in October 1992, along with the presence of the representatives of UNPROFOR, the JNA withdrew from that region and that this was taken note of and recognised by the members of the United Nations as respect for the agreements that had been reached and signed. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am aware of the fact that the JNA did withdraw sometime in mid-1992. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this entire area of Konavle, more than 20 years ago, was where the JNA set up the first defence line and built up a series of warehouses and underground channels from which it was possible to put up resistance to far superior forces? And this was all within the concepts of the defence of Yugoslavia as a country at that time. That is to say 20 years ago, more than 20 years ago. And that is where the military had their army installations and that the JNA exclusively wished to retain control over their military installations in that region, that that's what its task was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. And do you know this: That it was precisely in that region where those clashes took place later on that there were large stockpiles of weapons in the warehouses of the Territorial Defence, in keeping with the concept that I have just put forward, and that those weapons were in fact used by all parties in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know one thing and that is that the weapons of the Civil Defence forces were not in Dubrovnik because it was moved to the barracks in Trebinje. I don't know exactly when, but I know that it was sometime in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that one of the basic aims of the JNA was to evacuate the people and combat technology and materiel from the areas in which it was subject to hostile enemy activity, and you yourself know about the blockades of the barracks throughout Croatia that were effected, that communications were cut and things like that done. So are you aware, then, that above all, the JNA wanted to protect and defend its own people, to evacuate the people from those areas, and to create conditions for a peaceful solution to be reached?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that that is true. I don't think that the JNA needed to evacuate anything from that area because there was no military materiel there. The way in which they wanted to protect and defend somebody, I think that that borders on madness rather than being a form of protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. You say yourself, and there's no question there, that Dubrovnik is of exceptional importance culturally speaking, touristically, and so on and so forth. Now, do you really think that it was a good idea to militarise Dubrovnik and to shoot from Dubrovnik at the army in the broader Dubrovnik region which, as you know full well, the first garrison was very near and so is the border with Montenegro. It's all nearby. Do you think that anything, any of this would have taken place had there not been violence and shooting coming from Dubrovnik, from the Dubrovnik area, shooting at the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think anything would have happened, but vice versa. I think everything would have been solved much more quickly and easily had the army not shot at Dubrovnik. I'm sure that much would have been preserved, many lives would have been saved had it been otherwise, had the army not shot at Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that the mayor of Dubrovnik, Petar Poljanic, who was here in this courtroom a little while ago, on the 12th of October, 1991, before TV cameras, stated that 15.000 shells fell upon Dubrovnik, and the whole world heard that news item, it travelled the world. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I think he was 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the very next day, which is to the say the 13th of October - he made the statement on the 12th of October - on the 13th, a meeting was held of the military maritime sector of Boka with the representatives of the municipality and representatives of the European Monitoring Mission precisely in Miocici which you mention. It is a village above Cavtat. When a member of the monitoring mission, observers, Adrian Stinger, said to journalists, he made a positive assessment of the meeting and said that he did not have knowledge of the fact that so many shells fell on Dubrovnik, although he himself lived in Dubrovnik and that he didn't even know that there was -- there were any casualties or that anyone was killed in Dubrovnik. Does that mean anything to you? Does it ring a bell? Does it say anything to you, information of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, information of that kind tells me nothing. I don't know what kind of judgement the Trial Chamber will bring in, but you can visit the cemetery in Dubrovnik, near Dubrovnik, when you come round, and you'll see the graves of 20 young men who laid down their lives for Dubrovnik, and the JNA killed them in their best years when they should have been in discotheques and been having a good time. They were forced to take up arms and defend their home town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry that those young men were killed, but they were not -- their death was not caused by the JNA but by that nonsensical idea that violence be used to effect violent secession, which could have been effected politically, through peaceful means, without any shots being fired, and you know that very well yourself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me add one more word: I think that your crazy idea killed them, your crazy idea about Greater Serbia, if I might say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting rather far from this witness's evidence. Let's get back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where do you get this idea about a Greater Serbia? Did you hear that somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, that's the very point I have in mind. We're getting far from his evidence. He gave evidence about specific events. I've allowed you to ask questions which have gone rather further, but there's no point in asking this witness about matters such as that. We'll hear other evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go back, Mr. May, to the evidence and testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know - and Croatian radio broadcast this at the beginning of November 1991, so I assume you do - a statement made by the Defence Minister, and I'm quoting: "All citizens of the Dubrovnik municipality who are not mobilised into the Croatian army civilian defence and who do not have a labour duty are duty-bound to report to the secretariat," et cetera, et cetera. So all the others were already mobilised into the Dubrovnik or, rather, Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 21st of October, they were all volunteers, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's not go into the details of all that, because you didn't testify about it, actually. But I'm sure you read about it. You must have read a book written by your commander, the commander on that Dubrovnik battleground, and it's called "All My Battles." And in that book, he describes rather differently this entire operation and the events that took place.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite frank and say that I haven't read the book. I think that I have seen enough and experienced and lived through enough that I don't actually need to read a book like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, then, that on the 22nd of October, in the fighting in Mlini that took place only a few kilometres, some ten kilometres away from Dubrovnik, that eight members of the JNA were killed? On the next day, the 23rd of October, in Ivanjica, another case in point, eight JNA members were killed. Ivanjica is in the Herzegovina area. How far, as the crow flies, is it from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually, but as the crow flies, it's about 10 kilometres away from Dubrovnik. But on the 21st of October, I had already been taken prisoner, so I really am not competent of talking about those events, I didn't hear about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is Ivanjica a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the ethnic composition of the population was. All I know is that Ivanjica is on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I really don't know who lived in Ivanjica. I might have visited Ivanjica once or twice because, before the war, there was a department store that sold furniture, so we went to buy some furniture there, and that's what I know about Ivanjica. As to the population there, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that it was razed to the ground as well? And who could have razed it to the ground, I ask you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period, the period we're discussing now and that I'm testifying to, it had not then been razed to the ground. That is for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't go to the department store once it had been razed, I assume.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that on the 28th of October in 1991, your year, in 1991, the year you're testifying about, that Dubrovnik was visited by more than 100 domestic and foreign journalists? They came to -- on the ship Argus, under the Red Cross flag. The first organised visit took place after several months since the conflict broke out. They came to Dubrovnik, and this was organised by this naval sector from the Bay of Boka Kotor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was already at the Bileca camp at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But did you hear about it? Did you learn that all the reporters noted that Dubrovnik had not been subjected to any great damage, especially not older inner city that was under UNESCO protection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I can't answer that question. All I can say and what I know about that period, which is the end of October and beginning of November, is that the guards and the officers that interrogated me said that they -- Dubrovnik would be taken by force if it didn't surrender of its own free will. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. In that very frustrating episode, I don't want to ask you anything about that. I don't want to even ask a single question about that frustrating period of your life. But I don't think it's very relevant as to what some non-commissioned officer, junior officer told you about Dubrovnik. Now, do you know that on the 28th of October [Realtime transcript read in error "2nd"], BBC and Sky Television, from London, broadcast the readiness of the Dubrovnik authorities to accept the conditions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on the 28th of October, although I see it's on the 2nd of October on the monitor, in the transcript, but when was it that you were taken into custody? Just remind us of that, would you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 21st of October, 1991, I was taken into custody, and I really can't answer questions of this kind because I wasn't there. I wasn't present, nor did I have any opportunity of hearing whether it took place and what took place or what didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm asking you about this piece of information. It was publicised, and they said that in Dubrovnik there were about 2.000 guardsmen and a large number of foreign mercenaries, and they published this piece of information on the 28th of October. I assume that on the 21st, when you were taken into custody, the situation could not have differed much from that. So this piece of information, this fact that was broadcast, was that incorrect and untruthful, namely that there were not 2.000 guardsmen and foreign mercenaries in Dubrovnik that shot at the army but just the hundred people that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can answer that question. It's a specific one. There were only those 100 people. There were no foreign mercenaries and there were no 2.000 guardsmen. It's ludicrous to talk about that. I read about that in some Serbian newspapers but I stand behind what I've said, that there were only 100 defenders of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't quote Serbian papers of any kind, I quoted Western sources. And do you know that one of the witnesses, I can't remember just now which one, and I quoted him here, I quoted from his statement, the witness statement given to the opposing side, the side that questioned you a moment ago, and he said that there were 500. Now, I don't know whether you aligned your views as to how many people were actually there to defend Dubrovnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stand by what I said, and the answer I gave. If somebody saw things differently, I don't know about that, but as far as I know, there were approximately 100 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And tell me, then, do you know whether there was a single official statement or decision taken by any organ of authority or on the part of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Montenegro, which borders on Croatia, or the ruling political parties in them which then or ever denied the notorious fact that Dubrovnik was a Croatian town in the Republic of Croatia, that it belongs to Croatia, and that no one had any pretensions towards it, towards taking it? Do you know of a single statement on the part of anyone, denying this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly to be able to quote anybody's statement, but I do know that there were considerable pretensions towards Dubrovnik, even when there were negotiations not to have the army enter, and then the army made several demands - I don't know exactly which - but that a flag of the Dubrovnik Republic should be flown and that it should not be under Croatian authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army never asked for Dubrovnik to become a Dubrovnik Republic. Do you remember, because at the time you were still not captured, that the Presidency of Montenegro and the government of Montenegro, on the 2nd of October, in a joint statement - which means 20 days before you were captured - they said that Montenegro was not at war but that it exclusively supported the JNA in defending the constitutional order and preventing the civil war from escalating? Do you know that? You must have heard that because you were a free man, and you must have heard what the Montenegrins said at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me give you a different answer to your question. In this Tribunal, I would like to state -- I could state that I am not a man but that I am a woman, and this will appear in the press and that is what we will read. So anyone can say whatever they wish. But the facts are there. The facts are those that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you're inclined, in favour of facts, let's me ask you, do you know, Mr. Hausvicka -- you mentioned that you recognised some locals from Dubrovnik in the military units when you were taken into custody. Do you know that Bruno Karmincic and that Dragan Gajic, Judges of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. District Court in Dubrovnik who carried out most of the investigations in the area of Dubrovnik regarding the destruction of property of the local Serbs, that these two investigating Judges in the District Court in 1991 carried out dozens of on-site inspections because of violence against inhabitants of Serb ethnicity, burning and destruction of houses, looting, et cetera? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer that question too, if that can be considered a question at all. The Serbs in Dubrovnik who stayed in Dubrovnik in those days and who are still living in Dubrovnik, can testify that no one ever mistreated them or persecuted them. And I personally have Serb and Montenegrin friends in Dubrovnik. So what you're saying is absolutely wrong, as far as I know. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just referring to the reports that my associates have collected, drawn up by Judges of the District Court of Dubrovnik and not by anyone from Serbia. That's why I'm asking you whether they're correct. If you're saying they're not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true that local criminals, in October 1991 - and you were in the police, so you must have known that - were released from prison and included in the armed formations that were opening fire on the army in the surroundings of Dubrovnik? Is that true or not, that local criminals, in October 1991, were set free and included in those units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is not true, because there's no prison in Dubrovnik. There is only detention on remand. So the prisons were outside Dubrovnik. And there may have been two or three people held in custody, but this is of no significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is a prison on the last floor of the District Court.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But listen, that is not a prison. That is a temporary detention before he's taken to trial. So there can be no more than three or four, maybe five men in there. But this could not represent any significant force for the defence of Dubrovnik, even if somebody had released them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, Mr. Hausvicka, is it true that fire was opened on JNA members not only from positions outside the old city but also within the city walls from a number of trucks on which anti-aircraft guns had been mounted? And JNA positions constantly shelled at Zarkovica and other localities around Dubrovnik. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a competent answer because I was already in detention. But regarding the 21st of October, no fire was opened from outside the old town or within the old town on JNA positions. I can say that up to the 21st of October. After that, I cannot -- someone else who was in town at the time could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me ask you, for the period prior to the 21st of October, is it true that as early as the 30th of September, 1991, you set up positions or front lines 700 metres long from Brgat to St. Barbara hills, and that from those positions, members of the ZNG, the police and armed civilians forming platoons were constantly opening fire on JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer the question. I wasn't there at those positions, but I can tell you one thing: On the 30th of September, the Serbs from Bileca and Trebinje who worked in Dubrovnik came to work on that day. So had there been any Croatian formations there, they couldn't have come to work. And of course, on the 1st of October when the attack on Dubrovnik started, nobody came. And some Serbs in Trebinje even gave some intimation of the forthcoming attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I just asked you is not true, that on the 30th of September there was a front line from Brgat to St. Barbara hill, including the National Guard Corps and civilian forces opening fire on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: I cannot tell you because I was in Mokosica. So I really don't know whether those positions existed or not. But I'm telling you what I know, that up to the 30th of September, cars came in and out of Dubrovnik normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that fire was opened on the JNA even from old bunkers that were left over from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they open fire from the belfry of the Saint Anne church?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot gave you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that from the town of Dubrovnik itself, fire was opened from positions near the Neptun Hotel by members of the National Guards? There was an anti-aircraft gun. Then also from the Lapadska Glavica, where there was another anti-aircraft gun. Gorica, another gun; Gradacac; the Ploce beach. Again these same guns. The Belvedere and Libertas hotels, where armed and uniformed members of paramilitary forces, as they were then, were located. Now, I've listed all these places. And tell me that there were -- that none of this was true.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of October until the 21st of October, those guns, I think, were not there. Later on, they were no longer paramilitary forces. They were forces of the Republic of Croatia defending Dubrovnik, and there may have been guns later on, but I think this was much later, in 1992. But at the beginning of October, I can guarantee that there wasn't a single gun in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you mentioned a moment ago that you did your military service in Serbia. And as a soldier serving in Serbia, did you have any kind of problems? I don't mean just in the barracks, but generally when you moved around town, when you went out, did you have any problems with civilians or with anyone or anywhere, any kind of problems of an ethnic nature just because you were a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be very specific. I did my military service in Sombor and then I was transferred to Kopaonik. This is a tourist resort, and in a shop I was a soldier, I went to buy something, I can't remember what, and at the cashier, the woman asked me, "Where are you from?" and I said, "From Croatia," and he said, "Get lost, you Ustasha." And that was the single unpleasantness I experienced. In Sombor, I didn't have any such experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You joined the National Guards Corps in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in response to an announcement in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even before there were any kind of pronounced tensions, and especially no violence, you joined the National Guards Corps as an armed formation of the HDZ. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're not right. In Slavonia, the war was raging by then, and there were expectations that something could happen in Dubrovnik too. But my joining the National Guard Corps was more emotional than anything else. As you called it, an HDZ force. I was a 20-year-old young man and I somehow felt privileged to be a member of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, I understand that, but are you disputing that it was an armed force of the HDZ when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are not right. The HDZ was in power in Croatia then, just as you were in power in Serbia. Forces were being formed because the war was well under way in Slavonia by then, so that all over Croatia, units of the National Guards Corps started to be formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that you responded to an advertisement in the newspapers and on television when you joined, as you told us yesterday. So tell me, who was it that was publishing these announcements and broadcasting these announcements to mobilise you to the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, so I really can't remember the exact wording. Nobody forced us to join the National Guards Corps, but whoever wanted to. Nobody forced anyone. As far as I know, even later on, though I was in detention by then, there was no general mobilisation in Dubrovnik, it was more on a voluntary basis. Joining the guards and the police was mostly on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the recruiting centre that you reported to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I think it was the Rasica villa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, were there any kind of criteria established for joining the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that the only positions of the Croatian police and army in 1991 were in Brgat, Osojnik, and Debeli Brijeg, which means along the border with Montenegro; is that right? Is it true that those units, on 31st of July, 1991, carried out works to close the road and fortify the positions in the Debeli Brijeg region and that they opened fire onto aircraft of the JNA? Do you remember that? That was on the 31st of July, 1991. You fortified your positions and that is when you opened fire into the territory of Montenegro and on JNA planes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true -- so the units were not positioned there. Communication was not cut off. There were no fortifications. So none of what I have said is true.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say one thing for sure; that communications were not interrupted, and I think that all you're saying is incorrect, and this fortification on the 31st of July, I believe that those statements are not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know -- this wasn't on a continuous basis but on several occasions -- on the 28th of August, 1991, these same units cut off communication lines with Montenegro and brought troops to Debeli Brijeg near the village of Prsecina, there were about 200 members of the National Guards Corps. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer because I wasn't there at the time. So I can't say whether there were 200, 300, or 100 of them. But as far as I know, transport flowed normally, that cars went to and from Montenegro normally. I don't know until what date exactly, but I think up to a few days prior to the attack on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that these 200 ZNG members were not there on the border at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say yes or no. I just said that I couldn't give you an exact answer. But as far as I know, I think that they were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And to the best of your knowledge, on the 14th of September in Debeli Brijeg, were obstacles put up and the environs mined by the members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I don't know. You're asking me things that I really don't know about. I can tell you more about the region around Mokosica and Old Mokosica. I don't know what was happening in the area of Debeli Brijeg. But according to what I know, I don't think there were any mines planted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that on the 23rd of September, members of the police and the ZNG, again your Dubrovnik forces, placed mortars and guns in Viteljina and provoked the JNA by opening fire on JNA positions in the territory of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you a concrete answer: If we had mortars and guns at the time, the army wouldn't have reached where it reached a month later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same happened on the 24th of September in the Ivanjica area.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat again: If we had had guns and mortars in those days, the army would not have advanced to where it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, as you keep claiming that the JNA was shelling you on the 2nd of October, that already then it had taken up positions above Mokosica, that you didn't engage in conflict with the JNA, who killed all these people on the Dubrovnik theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you a specific answer, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do. You give whatever answer you will, and that's up to you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, it's time for the adjournment. Have you any more questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, a few more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can have up to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, have you anything for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone does not appear to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes. If the senior legal officer would accompany us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Hausvicka, you say that I killed those people. All right. Although I think you should know that Serbia had absolutely nothing to do with that whole affair involving Dubrovnik. But with respect to the statement you signed and you say was 50 pages long, do you claim that none of these crimes that you signed your name to in that statement, that you did not perpetrate them yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed something that I didn't see, but what I signed I got from the guards because they had read it. So I don't know what was written in that statement, in that book, but what I claim is that it wasn't how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what it says in those 50 pages, but you signed it; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I signed it, that I heard from the guards that -- about what was written inside, but I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were taken prisoner and when that man from Dubrovnik who asked you whether you knew him, you recognised him, and when he identified himself, he said that you went around town slaughtering women and children. Did he -- is that something he fabricated, he thought up on the spot?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm not going to ask you what you did. There will be other people testifying here. But I shall respect the comment or, rather, the suggestion that was made by Mr. May, and I shall refrain from asking this witness anything about those frustrating events, although -- so I only have several more questions to ask him. As it has not been challenged that you were registered as a prisoner of war and that you were regularly supervised as a prisoner of war by the Red Cross, is it logical to you that in that supervision performed by the Red Cross at least something would have been seen of all those amazingly large quantities of beatings and abuse that you suffered? They would have seen something of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they saw enough. So I don't think that is a problem. Everybody knows who visited the camp, and I'm sure those people will be able to testify about it, because when the representatives of the Red Cross came to visit, it is true that several days prior to their visit the beatings were lesser, but the scars and traces of the beatings could be -- were evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you explain that the Red Cross makes no mention of beatings of the type that you describe and the ill-treatment and everything else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't read -- haven't read their report, so I can't say. I can't answer that question of yours. I never read those reports, but what I experienced and lived through I think I have described sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask you any more about that. Just tell me this: Where do you see the logic in all of this, in what you're claiming; that they would even come from Bileca to this Miocici or whatever the name of the place was where you were detained, and the journey last several hours, to beat you there. Why would they come all the way from Bileca to beat you in your new camp?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why, but the sergeant, staff sergeant, did come by. I don't know whether they were bringing anybody else into the camp.
