The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. camp was composed of several sheds, so I don't know how many detainees there were in total there, but I think they came in to remind us of their existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hausvicka, when were you released?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of September, 1992, and the exchange took place in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then all those subsequent years you worked in the Special Police Units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked until mid-1994. And because of the repercussions of what had happened to me, I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So from 1992 to 1994, that is to say two years, you worked in the units of the special police force. And allegedly these disturbances that you suffered didn't prevent you from carrying out your work and doing that kind of job for two years.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a doctor to be able to answer your questions professionally, but the psychological stress that occurs not set in straight away but it is a delayed reaction. I, at the time, felt psychologically capable, and perhaps I wanted to take my revenge slightly, but in 1994, my psychological breakdown started and I had to undergo psychological treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you started to feel the psychological disorders and disturbances two years later?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, psychological disturbances and other symptoms that I didn't pay much attention to, but my spine was injured, my kidneys were injured, my ribs and head. I didn't attach too much importance to that because that was physical pain. But psychological pain I began to experience in 1994 when I applied for treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me just once again: Do you claim that you did not kill a single person?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I say, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to ask you to be -- give the prisoner -- give the witness, I beg your pardon, a copy of his witness statement. There are differences in the statement he made then and in the testimony he has given in court today. So I should like to ask him to explain some of the details in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Copies are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have them. We should have them too. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first question for you, Witness, has to do with what is contained in your witness statement on page 1. It is paragraph 7. It's the same in the English version. You have already stated yesterday or today, I don't remember, that you joined the ZNG, the Croatian National Guard Corps, voluntarily. However, in the statement you gave to the investigators, you say, "I joined the Croatian National Guard on practically the first day that they started recruiting in Dubrovnik." You don't mention any volunteer -- any volunteering. You say that in May 1991, general recruitment had started for the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reading that sentence now. This was read out to me. I didn't happen to notice that, but this is not my own sentence. I didn't say that recruitment -- any kind of recruitment had started. I think that that was -- is an error in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is general recruitment that began and not that you wanted to join the ZNG voluntarily. You were recruited. So you're saying that's not true.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's not true. I think that has been erroneously written down and I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the following paragraph, you said that there were about 100 men in the ZNG. Is it true that you did not have any uniforms and were wearing civilian clothes at the time, as it says here, but that you were all issued with automatic rifles similar to the Kalashnikov type?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one or two months before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as it says in the following paragraph, that you were located in improvised barracks the whole time. So you were in military positions throughout.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were put up at the villa Rasica. It's not a barracks. I don't know why it says that. It was actually a hotel, or a holiday centre. And that's where we were accommodated. We slept there and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is what it says in the following paragraph true? You say, "I left the ZNG and, in August 1991, joined the unit of the Croatian special police in Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Most of my friends were there or, rather, a number of my friends were already there, and I joined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to the automatic rifle, you were issued a pistol as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were there in those special Croatian police units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that: There were about 50 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know one more point that is not contained in your statement which you gave to the investigators, and that is the following: That the Defence Minister of Croatia had already on the 18th of July, as you are a young man, in 1990, brought in a rule according to records for volunteer youth units, recording their names?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You don't know about that. And do you know when the Croatian National Guard Corps started being formed? Was it prior to the conflict in Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say something else in your statement which you failed to recall when you were asked here today. In your witness statement, on page 3, paragraph 4 of the English version - and the B/C/S version, in that version it is the same page, the same paragraph, in fact - you say that you do not know about the positions that existed along the border towards Montenegro. And here you say: "To my knowledge, the only Croatian military or police positions at the time were in Brgat, Osojnik, and Debeli Brijeg, all border crossings towards Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer today was to the gentleman too that I cannot answer that question competently. I did know that there exist, but not military ones, police checkpoints or crossings, or whatever you like to call them, at Osojnik, Debeli Brijeg, and Brgat. I'm thinking about the border crossings, that there were checkpoints there. That's as far as I know. I wasn't actually there so I can't confirm who and what was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you were quite categoric in saying that they were military positions. That's what you said at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was wrongly translated. I think that I emphasised that they were police positions because there was no army in Dubrovnik at that time, no military at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in knowing things related to the fact that you were taken into custody. You said you were armed when you were arrested and that you had weapons, but you didn't say everything you had with you. You had a rifle, two hand grenades --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rifle, two hand grenades, a pistol, and a knife -- a bayonet, in fact; a knife on my rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you go on to say in the following paragraph that you were arrested by JNA soldiers but that these were actually reservists.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing uniforms of the JNA army. Some of them had beards, others did not and were clean-shaven, so I assumed they were reservists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to explain to the Trial Chamber the following: You said that after that, you were taken off to Osojnik first, and then you went on to describe what you experienced there, and you were alone. Is that right? Were you alone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer. I don't know what you mean by "alone."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were no other detainees, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the barracks in Trebinje, you were mostly alone there too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was completely alone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you arrived in Bileca, where you spent seven months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 7, the last paragraph of the English version, which is also page 7, paragraph 5 of the B/C/S version, you state the following and I would like to ask you if it was correct: "I was in a solitary confinement cell for the first 10 to 15 days." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you say that you were put up in a room where there were 10 other civilians.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they civilians or were they once again persons who were deprived of their freedom, taken into custody the same way you were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were predominantly elderly persons, between the ages of 50 and 60, who were brought in there from the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me this now, please: You say that in the following days, the maximum figure was about 15.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the room I was in, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on page 8, paragraph 3, which is also paragraph -- which is the one but last paragraph in the English version: "I remained with a group of about 10 prisoners, mostly civilians. I believe that there were other prisoners around the camp but, as I had not really seen them, I cannot be sure of it."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come, in response to Mr. Nice's question, you said that there were 200 detainees in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't see all the 200 prisoners, but according to the information I gained later on, I understood that in the sports hall there were some more detainees, 150 to 180 persons, in fact. And I live in Dubrovnik. We all know -- all of us know each other who went through Bileca. I was there with the 15 but there were many more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people from Mokosica were with you there among those 200 individuals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Mokosica, I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the 200 people that were put up in the bomb shelters.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only you from Mokosica, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, in the statement you gave in the year 2000 you did not mention the number of people that were there? You don't say that anywhere in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. What did I not state?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you stayed on with about 10 detainees, and then you go on to say on page 9, for example - it is the third paragraph from the top, page 9 and 10 - that, "Sometime in December 1991, several other detainees arrived from Bosnia," and you say that very precisely. Not 200, you just say several.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me the page of that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is page 9, paragraph two from the bottom. Penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think it is ludicrous to have this translation saying "several." "Several" means two or three. But detainees were brought in on a massive scale at that time. I saw at least 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is a poor translation and that you didn't say what it says here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to say who did this translation and who did it wrong, but I didn't follow the text of it and this seems to be rather funny. I know that I saw at least 100 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So instead of the "several," you say that it should state about a hundred; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on page 11, paragraph 3 of the English version, which is page 10 of the B/C/S version, the version you have in front of you, paragraph 5 to you, you state that about this time, a group of about 20 other prisoners arrived from Morinje and that there was talk of an exchange.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were all returned to the Morinje camp.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Morinje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you were all exchanged.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 2nd of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness have Exhibit 336, the atlas, please. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to that, I think the very last answer to Mr. Tapuskovic reads the exchange was on the 2nd of July, 1991, in the transcript. I didn't note what was said by the witness but I think it was 1992 that you were exchanged; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd of July, 1992, in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you would open those -- if the usher would be good enough to open the atlas at page 37. You've been asked a number of questions about what the JNA was or was not doing. We took this somewhat quickly at an earlier stage. Was the advance on Dubrovnik from one or from more than one different directions, and if from more than one different directions, can you just point out to us on the map from where the JNA advanced on Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, from several directions. On the 1st or 2nd of October, I don't know exactly, Slano was occupied and the Adriatic highway was closed, so that already then Dubrovnik was surrounded, because at sea there was the navy and its ships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the navy was doing at that stage? Were you ever aware of whether or not there was such a thing as a blockade of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dubrovnik was blocked already on the 1st or 2nd of October. I really am not sure, it's one of those two days that Slano was taken. So Dubrovnik was blocked from the sea and from the land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the pointer, just show to the Judges so that there's no doubt about it, from which directions, in the plural, the JNA advanced on Dubrovnik. Was it from north, south, east, west, or from where?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about north, south, or east. It came from Slano, from Osojnik, from Ivanjica, and from Montenegro, from Konavle, towards Dubrovnik; and from the sea, there was the navy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's been suggested to you by the accused that attacks were initiated on the JNA by Croats. Was there anything that you saw or heard of to support that suggestion of the accused that Croats initiated attacks on the JNA, on the army itself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, none of that is true. But as for the area I was in, I can say with certainty that there were no provocations on the Croatian side against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described, in respect of the area to the north and east of Mokosica and others have described in respect of other parts of the nearby area, the JNA being on high ground, in a position to overlook either Mokosica or Dubrovnik. Was there any need that you could see for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the army to be out of its barracks, placed in those strategic positions on high ground, overlooking the areas that were shelled? Was there any need for them to be there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, they shouldn't have been there. If they hadn't been there, there wouldn't have been a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA publicly justify in any way its presence on these high ground positions, that you can recall? If so, just tell us what they said about them. If they said nothing, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean through the mass media?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I really didn't hear anything so I can't say anything; I don't think they said anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused used the term that there was a "violent secession" by Croatia. In your area, was there any question of a violent secession?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no signs of any such thing. Croatia, at the time, carried out a referendum when the Croatian people opted in favour of secession. I don't remember the exact date because it was a long time ago, but I don't think anything was done that would warrant an aggression against the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the accused also suggested to you that there was hostile enemy activity justifying JNA evacuation of people in the areas that were attacked. Was there any hostile enemy activity of which you were aware, by the Croats, that could have justified JNA evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused suggests that there is in existence an order not to attack Dubrovnik. He didn't show you such an order. We'd be grateful to see it if he has it with him, but tell us, please, have you ever heard of or seen any such order not to attack Dubrovnik made by someone on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with that topic, it's been suggested that the president of Montenegro issued a statement that they were not at war with Croatia or with Dubrovnik, I'm not sure which. Do you have any recollection of that statement of the president of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember any such statement by the president of Montenegro. I can just say one thing, that that same president had a picture taken with the so-called defenders of Dubrovnik on the top of a hill when the JNA had an overview of Dubrovnik, a bird's-eye view of Dubrovnik from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think just help us, please; did that same president also issue an apology later in respect of what he had in fact been a party to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The current President of Montenegro, yes; and the former one, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The former one was Bulatovic, and the present one is Djukanovic. They were both involved at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we, in light of the allegations that have been put by the accused, now see the apology that has been made? I've got the tape ready and transcripts available, to reflect the Montenegrin view. It's quite short. Although the transcript is two pages, the passage we require is only about a couple of inches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll see that for completeness, I've provided the whole of the transcript of the relevant television programme, but we need go only down to the end of the first half of the page, where we have the two quotations by or passages by --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to comment, as an amicus, that I think that it is not appropriate to bring this in through this witness. The witness has not confirmed that he heard it. And secondly, this is a paragraph that is being offered through this witness and it is not appropriate. I think we should wait for some other occasion to present this to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's nothing to do with the public. It's being presented to this Court, Mr. Tapuskovic. Remember that. Now, we play videos and the like, usually, and the relevance, as I understand it, is that allegations were put by the accused in cross-examination as to the attitude of Montenegro. Yes. Just a moment. Let Mr. Nice respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. Those are the allegations that have been made. Here is a document that goes to show either the genuine or the corrected version by Montenegro of its attitude. And indeed, I think the accused is clearly aware of the broadcast. Whether he's seen it or not is probably not entirely critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has in fact confirmed that the president made the apology, so I think it is entirely appropriate to have it put through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to admit it. If the relevant passage could be played. You were going to tell us where the relevant passage is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the first page and I think it's queued right to the beginning there. So all we need go to is from the beginning, where it says "News Editor" down to the second passage of Mr. Djukanovic, which is halfway down the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's some problem about showing it, apparently. It hasn't got an audio attached. Do you want to show it? Perhaps the simplest thing is to show it very quickly without the audio and you can refer us to the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. If we can see the video, we can pick up probably the relevant passage and I can read from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here we see the newscaster. We there see Mr. Djukanovic and Mr. Mesic, talking together. This is part of the opening passage with an account, and here is the words of Mr. Djukanovic, and he said this -- and I'll get a version which can be played with audio soon. He says: "I would like to use this opportunity and on my behalf and on behalf of the citizens of Montenegro, particularly those citizens who share my broader political and moral views, express my deepest regrets to the Croatian citizens, particularly to the citizens of Konavle, Dubrovnik, and Neretva county, for all the pain, suffering and material losses that were inflicted upon them by any citizen of Montenegro as a member of the Yugoslav national army during those tragic events." The reporter returns to the screen and makes this point: "Presidents Mesic and Djukanovic assessed today's meeting as extremely important for security in the whole region. For the Montenegrin president, it is in line with Montenegro's search for the constitutional status and identity." And Mr. Djukanovic is then seen again, and we can probably actually stop the tape now, thank you, because we've moved on, but Mr. Djukanovic is then seen saying: "Unfortunately, the regime in Serbia has not given up the ambition to keep Montenegro in the cage of its unrealistic, monstrous, centralist, and dictatorial projects."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date, please, of this broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's -- I'm so sorry not to have the date immediately at hand. I'll make it available before the end of the morning, probably before I've sat down. I think it's last year, but I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The last comment is a contemporary one and is of really no relevance; however, the other one, of course, we'll take account of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm wrong; it's the 25th of June, 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And help us, please, Mr. Hausvicka: Did you see that apology screened in 2000 yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the video be given an exhibit number but on the basis that rather than trouble you with one with and one without audio, I'll ensure that the one you have has an audio, so that the one with audio becomes an exhibit, and may the transcript bear an associated exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the transcript should have an A number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 365A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm invited to correct what may have been misapprehension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Hausvicka, it was President Bulatovic who was photographed on the Dubrovnik front and the person making the apology is the more recent president, Djukanovic, now Prime Minister of Montenegro. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few more questions. There was reference to bearded soldiers and reference to paramilitary forces. Were there bearded soldiers whom you saw, and how did they react to or how did they seem to be controlled by the clean-shaven JNA soldiers who you otherwise saw?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bileca camp, in addition to the regular army and reservists, there were some people -- I don't know how to call them. They had crossed belts in front, beards, and some strange insignia on their heads which were not JNA insignia. I don't know how to put it. These were groups out of control. And when we went to do labour, we were afraid because they would shoot and they would get drunk, and we feared they might attack us. They would use all kinds of words. Sometimes they would point guns at us. We didn't know what they could do to us, and I don't think that the guards would do anything to protect us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they, nevertheless, apparently under the direction of people at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, since they were there. I believe that they were under the command of those in the camp, because this was a military barracks and there was an army in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that topic there's been some suggestion at the first part of the accused's questioning there may have been something irregular about the soldiers who were dealing with you. When the ICRC, when the Red Cross came to the camp where you were held, was there any suggestion by anybody that this was anything other than a regular JNA establishment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact answer to that question. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your statement's been explored -- and, Your Honour, that ought to perhaps to have an exhibit number, not least for the following reason: I'm not going to ask you to go into any more detail of the maltreatment you suffered, but did you set out in more detail than has been provided to this Court the treatment meted out to you by the soldiers in the camps where you were held, in that statement and did you do so accurately?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, I gave more details in describing what had happened, though there were even worse cases and humiliations that I experienced that I don't wish to talk about in this court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope the statement may be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get a number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 366.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, in light of the very last answer, without reading it out publicly, I'll just invite Your Honours to look to page 7 as an example, the penultimate paragraph as opposed to the ultimate one, to reflect exactly the point that the witness has made, and I'm going to ask him to deal with one matter in light of one of the accused's suggestions, which can be found on page 10, I think. While I'm finding the right page for that, I may have missed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's suggested by the accused that the JNA was representing Yugoslavia as a whole and in a sense was represented on an even basis by various national groups. One incident, which is on page -- I'm grateful to Mr. Valieres-Roland, it's on page 8, in the middle of the page. Was there an occasion in the Bileca camp where a Cyrillic magazine was the subject of some treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A newspaper came out of the JNA. I think it was called Narodna Armija, and they would give us a page, or half a page, in Cyrillic, for us to learn it by heart in five, ten or 15 minutes, and if we didn't know it by heart, they would beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is all I need to ask of this witness save to tidy up one matter of detail in case it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the number of combatants in the shelter or shelters of which you've spoken, was the five or six combatants the total number of combatants in one shelter or in all six shelters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one shelter. Actually, in the area of Nova Mokosica, where there were five or six shelters, there were five of us; three special policemen and two ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the total number of policemen or ordinary policemen in the totality of the number of shelters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT HAUSVICKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hausvicka, that concludes your evidence. We're grateful to you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make a comment only on what Mr. Nice said a moment ago. Djukanovic is expressing regret because of the suffering provoked by citizens of Montenegro in that area, the citizens of Montenegro within the JNA. He does not express regret because of the defence of Yugoslavia but because of the unnecessary suffering provoked by certain citizens of Montenegro, and it is well known that there was looting and violence over there. Therefore, I think that the statement should be read correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will interpret that. It will be a matter for us, and in due course you can address us on it. When you come to the end of the case, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He confirms that there was a conflict between the JNA and the forces of Croatia in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The matter -- the matter has now passed. You can address us in due course on it. You can address us on it in due course. Yes. Mr. Nice, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness will be taken by Mr. McKeon. We do not have another witness after this witness. I've explained the reasons for that. If there is any spare time at the end of the morning, there may or may not be some administrative matters we could discuss. There probably won't be any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I doubt it. What we could do with is a list for next week's witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A list has been prepared this morning and is now being circulated. You will discover that we've only been able to fix witnesses for next week because of some of the administrative problems we're referring to and that were dealt with elsewhere in written material available to the Chamber. We're having difficulties the following week but of course we will fill that gap but we won't be able to notify parties until sometime next week who they'll be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May. Mr. Nice asked -- he put a question with respect to the order that I quoted, and I should like to give him that explanation or, rather, to give the explanation to you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. On the 4th of October, 1991, there is an order of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the General Staff, in fact, 1779-1 is the number of it, and in brackets it says: [as interpreted] "(126 of the 4th of the October 1991). Don't take over Dubrovnik or open artillery fire and air force fire on it." On the 4th of October, another order to block Dubrovnik precisely because of the shooting. Now I'm reading this from the documentation because Serbia didn't have anything to do with that whole affair but there are documents in the army. So this is an army [as interpreted] by the General Staff. "Do not take control of Dubrovnik or open fire from the artillery or the air. And block Dubrovnik and caution not to attack Dubrovnik on that same day." The Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the General Staff, and the number I mentioned, 4th of October, et cetera, 1991. And I assume that we can have those documents at our disposal. So it was a conflict between the JNA and the paramilitary units of Croatia, and the order by the General Staff not to attack Dubrovnik but just to block it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And all the rest is just pure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I take it from what you say, Mr. Milosevic, that you don't have the orders yourself. If you have them, let the Court have them. If not, no doubt inquiries can be made. Yes. We will have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, I wanted to direct your attention to the atlas, Exhibit 326, particularly page 23. This witness is going to be talking about the villages of Lovas, Tovarnik, and Ilok, which appear in grid E-2 on page 23 of the atlas.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit 336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McKeon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will be known in these proceedings as Witness C-1204. A piece of paper is now going to be put in front of you and I would like you to take a look at it, please, and answer yes or no whether the details on the piece of paper that are placed before you are correct.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, are you a Croatian by nationality, born in Vukovar in 1963, and did you live in Lovas, Croatia until the 24th of December, 1991, when you were forced to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, please, what the village of Lovas was like before the war, paying particular attention to what the ethnic composition was of the village between Croats and non-Croats.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It was a peaceful, quiet village. Most of the inhabitants were Croatians. Eight per cent were non-Croats. There were some Hungarians. The rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There were no problems. We all lived together and were friends. We grew up together, went to school together right up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far is the village of Lovas from the border between Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about two and a half to three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the non-Croats that lived in the village, of what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There were some Hungarians and some Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were most of the non-Croats Serbians or Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you describe for us when the first attack on Lovas occurred? Could you tell us about that attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It was autumn. The tanks were moving towards Vukovar across a field. We were picking apples in an orchard. We heard some shots, and they were targeting the village. Of course we were frightened, so we took refuge. We fled towards the village. And as we were approaching our Catholic church in the village, I saw that the steeple had been damaged from a tank grenade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they were firing shots," were these shots coming from the tanks or from guns or from something else?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: From the tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many shells were sent flying towards Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Several. Three or four. One hit and damaged the steeple of the church. The others missed the church but came in the same direction and fell on the outskirts of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this attack on Lovas, this tank attack, take place before or after the village of Tovarnik was taken over by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a second attack by tanks on Lovas, and if so, could you describe for us what happened during that second attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The same thing, after Tovarnik was taken over. Several days later they went up along the Sid-Vukovar main road and targeted the silos of the factory farm and also shot at the church and the steeple was set fire to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in either of those two tank attacks were any people in Lovas killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many shells would you estimate were sent at Lovas during this second tank attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Four to five pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the second tank attack took place a few days after the takeover of Tovarnik. How far from the village of Lovas is the village of Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it then that the village of Tovarnik was taken over before the village of Lovas was taken over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the takeover of Tovarnik, did the people from that village leave the village, and if so, did any of them come to your village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Most of them fled to Lovas. Some of them went towards Ilok. But for the most part, they were put up with friends and relatives in Lovas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did these people leave Tovarnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They explained to us that the tanks had enter the village and started firing. They targeted the church and set fire to it. They set fire to the Croatian houses, and the people fled because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that fled from Tovarnik to Lovas, were they Croats or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after Tovarnik was taken, was there a meeting that took place between villagers from Lovas with the JNA to discuss the possible surrender of the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There were talks. Four persons, four locals from the village, two Serbs and two Croats, went to Sid, and they talked to a JNA officer there, and he demanded that they hand over their weapons. He mentioned some 100 automatic rifles. However, there weren't any things of that kind, and there was general panic because the people knew what happened in Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "panic." You mean the people that went to this meeting or the people that were back in the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: In the whole village. There was panic throughout the village, because people were afraid. They were afraid that we would suffer the same fate as the neighbouring village of Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the four locals that went for this meeting with the JNA in Sid, were they Croats or were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Two of them were Croats, and the other two were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were in the village that you said were afraid because of what had happened to Tovarnik, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, they waited for night and left for Ilok. They didn't know where to go, actually. You couldn't go any further. You couldn't go to Vinkovci or Vukovar. So that they would shut themselves up in their houses and wait to see what was going to happen to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened the next day after this meeting in Sid?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The next day, the JNA officer arrived with a priest, a Catholic priest from Tovarnik. He came together with a driver, this JNA officer did, and the priest, and he made a lot of noise and shouted around and demanded that the weapons be handed over. And he said that the army would come in and search the houses for weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this JNA officer make any sorts of threats or statements about what might happen to the people of the village of Lovas if guns and weapons were not handed in, and if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, he threatened and said that the army would come in and that they would search the village and that we would suffer the same fate as Tovarnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the main attack on the village of Lovas take place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us that attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the morning, around 7.00 a.m., we heard explosions, and you could hear tanks firing and shells falling on the village. Then there was a certain lull. It was quiet for a few minutes. And then we heard a burst of gunfire coming from the direction of Opatovac. And we fled to the cellars. I lived in the centre, and so I looked out onto the street to see what was going on, and I saw that people wearing camouflage, with weapons, were moving around and that they were forcing some of the villagers in front of them to move on. I went back to the cellar, and several minutes later somebody came to the door. They shouted for me to come out of the cellar, otherwise they would throw a grenade on the house. So I came out of the cellar, I opened the gates and they came inside. I took my children out. And they kept shouting and making a lot of noise. And then one Serb turned up from the village. He was also with them, this Serb, and told them to leave, to go outside. And he came and asked me whether I had any weapons. I said I didn't, and he said there would be no problems and that I just put out a white sheet on my gate and not to leave my grounds, my property. And they continued down along the street. You could still hear some shooting. And that's what happened. I stayed in my yard and didn't leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the reason why you had to put a white sheet on your house?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, so that we could mark the house as having been searched and to say that we were Croats living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the other houses in the village that belonged to Croats, were they also required to put white sheets on them and were white sheets also put on the homes that belonged to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: All the Croatian houses had to display the white sheets, but the not Serbs houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the days after the takeover of Lovas, were you required to wear anything on your clothing to identify you yourself personally as a Croat?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: When we moved around the village, we had to have a white piece of cloth around our arms, tied to our arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we had to have that," is that the Croatian residents had to have the white piece of cloth on their arms?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, only the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb residents of the village, did they have to wear anything on their clothing to identify themselves?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the attack on your village started with a tank -- tank shells followed by a lull and then by a burst of gunfire. How long did the tank barrage take before the individual gunfire started in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Several minutes. Several shells fell, then they stopped so that their people could come into the village and not run the risk of being shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said "so their people could come in." You saw some of these people that were going around the village. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that you saw, were they local Serbs -- well, first of all, could you tell us -- could you describe them for us?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were wearing parts of uniforms, medical uniforms, civilian, army ones. They had weapons, all kinds of weapons, the Zolja type of rifle, semi-automatic rifles, automatic rifles. They were sort of unkempt, untidy looking, and there were locals of my village too, but there were other people we didn't know. Then there were some others from other villages whom I knew from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the local people you knew, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they travelling together with the other people that you didn't know or were they going in groups by themselves, the locals in one group and the non-locals from outside the village in another group?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were mixed, because they would indicate and point out the Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this initial period on the first day, did you see any soldiers that you could identify as regular or reserve JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, towards evening the tanks arrived in the village, and they deployed around the village, and some ten buses arrived too, army buses, and ten army trucks too with all the attending equipment. There were reservists there. There were young soldiers there wearing regular uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the tanks enter the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Towards evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the busloads of JNA soldiers come into the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: After them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the tanks came into the village, however, on that first day were there any JNA soldiers that you saw in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I didn't see any, but then I didn't dare go out onto the street. So we watched through the windows as much as we could see, but it wasn't advisable to look out of your window because they would shoot around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this attack on the 10th of October, was Lovas defended by villagers shooting back at the people that came in or was it basically left undefended?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It was taken over without any defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were killed during this attack on Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there anything that you can tell us about the people that were killed such as were they young, were they old, male, female, anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Most of them were elderly people. Three women were killed in the streets where they came across them, and some of them were 35 years of age. The others were 60, 65.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were killed during this attack, were they killed by the shells that were fired by the tanks, or were they killed by bullets and being shot?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: As far as I know, just one man was killed in his yard by a shell. The shell fell in his yard. All the rest were killed by bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when these ten busloads of JNA soldiers arrived in the village, where did they go? Did they remain in the village, and were they housed in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were housed in the primary school building and towards the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exits of the village. They asked to be in the Croatian houses and be nearer the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croatian houses that they were housed in, what happened to the people that lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They just turned them out of their homes and told them to fend for themselves and go to other people's houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Serbs thrown out of their homes so that the JNA could stay in their houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were checkpoints set up by the JNA around the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes. At the exits to the village at several points, there were checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it possible to leave the village once these checkpoints were set out -- up, without passing through JNA checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: On the first night, that was still possible, because some of the villagers who lived at the ends of the villages were able to flee. But afterwards, those checkpoints were better manned and control was more rigorous, and you couldn't leave after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that left after the attack, where did they go to, and what percentage of the population left the village after the attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Most of them fled to Ilok, and all in all, about 60 per cent of the people fled, some during the first day on the attack, and others during that first night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the village, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I did not leave the village. I lived in the centre, so I couldn't move around anywhere. And I also had small children and my family, so I stayed with them. I didn't want to be separated from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the JNA soldiers and reservists that were in the village, were there any paramilitary-type groups that remained in the village, and if so, could you describe those groups that remained in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a number of them. They called themselves the Jovic men, or Jovicevci, Dusan Silni, the White Eagles, there was some Valjevci from Valjevo. All young men dressed the same way, wearing camouflage uniforms, well-armed, tidy-looking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the mix of these paramilitary forces versus the JNA? Were there more JNA forces, more paramilitary forces, were they roughly equal? If you could describe what the mix was of these forces in the village.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't count them; they were moving around. They would give us assignments. We had to work. But for the most part, the whole village was full of them. They would come and go. There was lots of comings and goings, but I would say that there were more JNA active soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these paramilitaries came and went from the village, did they have to pass through the JNA checkpoints to get into and out of the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the homes of Croatians during and after the attack on the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were -- when they entered, a lot of houses were set on fire. Then they would be stormed, looted. Any valuables would be taken; money, gold jewellery, household appliances, cars, things of that type.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the houses that belonged to the Serb residents also set on fire?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the houses that belonged to the Serb residents also looted?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did this looting of the houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Those paramilitary units. They looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any steps being taken by any of the JNA soldiers, regular or reservists, to attempt to stop these people from looting the Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the villagers had to work. What jobs were you given after the village was taken over?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I did some physical labour. We had to do that for several days. We would collect firewood for the furnace and stoves. And then several days later, a villager came up to me and said that I had to be a drummer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what a drummer does.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We go through the village, carrying a drum. He would beat the drum with a stick. He would be given a text to read out, and he had to go up and down the village along its streets and read out the text, make the announcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you in fact do that job?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the texts that you were given, were you able to learn who had assumed the position as president of the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Devetak have any official position in the village before the takeover of the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No. He was just a local villager, and he lived in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a local commander of the TO forces in the village? And if so, who was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There was, and his name was Milan Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, if you were able to tell us from the documents that you saw as the village announcer, who was commanding the JNA troops that were in the village after the village was taken over by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Captain Marko Kovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like -- I'd like to turn your attention now to the events of October 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, this starts at paragraph 19 of the proofing summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, sir, is just tell us in your own words what happened in the village on that day, starting with the announcement that was made for all men to report to the centre, the Zadruga building.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I was informed that I should pass on the message that the people should gather in the centre of the village at 6.00 p.m., all between 18 and 55 or 60 years of age, for some discussions and information. When the people gathered, I was among them. They surrounded us, and, one by one, they would push us into the yard of the mechanical workshop. There, they searched us in a rough way. They seized everything from us - cigarettes, lighters - and forced us to sit on benches lined up in two rows in the yard. They left us there all night. They registered us, they threatened us, they hit us. They would come round to see us during the night. On a piece of high ground there were machine-guns some 10 metres away from us, and they threatened if anybody moved they would kill us. And they would make their rounds during the night, hit with us rifle butts on the back, on the head, in the kidney area, so that we experienced a lot of fear and a lot of blows that night. It was quite cold, so that in the morning we were all frozen. But we survived that night, and we hoped that things would get better, that they wouldn't kill us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: In the morning --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this before we get on to what happened in the morning: The order that people should gather, the men should gather, who signed that order?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us make it clear. Was it all the people or all the men who should gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was, was it not, the men that were of a certain age? I think you mentioned between the ages of 18 and 55; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Between 18 and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were gathered together in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned, when you started to describe this, that "they surrounded us, they held machine-guns on us." Could you tell us who it was who was holding you and these other men prisoners.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Valjevci. Men from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these JNA regular or reserve soldiers or were they a paramilitary group that you called Valjevci?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I would say that they are regulars, because they were all about the same height, well-built, like a special elite unit. They were disciplined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the night, were the 70 men allowed to lay down or stand up or change position, or were they forced to maintain the same position during the night?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We had to sit up straight, and we were not allowed to bend down or turn around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us what happened in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think before we get there, that might be a convenient moment. We're turning to a new topic. Witness C-1204, could you remember in this adjournment and any others there may be not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We're going to adjourn now for twenty minutes. Could you be back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I think -- I think we're up to the morning after the long night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened in the morning, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: In the morning, Devetak came, and the commander of the Valjevci. They called him Boxer. And a roll call started, and as people passed by them - they were lined up - they would hit him with rifle butts, iron bars, pieces of iron, so that people fell down bloodstained, with broken bones. And then they came across two brothers who were not there. They sent someone to fetch them home. They continued beating and hitting the people. And when these brothers were brought in, they started beating them straight away. One of them, whom they called Petronije, he hit Ante Luketic in the kidney area with a knife. The man fell. Blood flowed from him. They continued kicking him. And then they continued calling out names, and they stopped suddenly. They had some discussion and then they said that we would go with them outside the village to search the area for Ustashas. They lined us up in two columns. The boys that were beaten up stayed behind, lying on the ground. We went outside in two -- in two lines, and they accompanied us on both sides. When we came to the gate, there was a kind of ramp we passed. We went outside, and they went inside so that they explained if these opened fire, that they should hit us first and not them. And when we came to a bend, a boy had his pelvic bone broken. He couldn't walk any longer. They shouted that he had to move on. He said he couldn't, and he lagged behind, and we just heard a burst of fire, and the man was killed. We continued on our way, and we reached a clover field. They told us to go towards a hillock, and we had to hold hands and to trample on the clover with our feet, which was rather high, 30 centimetres high. Then we had to turn around and face the Borovo factory and go uphill. After about ten metres, we came across a wire. Somebody shouted out "wire." There was an explosion and then shooting. And they had told us before that that we mustn't lie on the ground. And out of fear because of the explosion and the shooting, I lay down and there were bullets whizzing by, and we could hear screams. And then they said that one of theirs, Joco, had been wounded. We stayed on the ground, lying down. Then they cared for him, and then they ordered us to get up. Those of us who got up, who hadn't been wounded, we got up. Those who had been wounded had to raise a hand, and they did. Then a military vehicle came by, a JNA vehicle, from the direction of the village. When it arrived, it stopped at the bend and they asked what had happened. And they said the Ustashas had planted a minefield and that we had come across it. And they said that it wasn't true, that the army had mined it, and that the wounded should be taken to the doctors and that we should be sent back. He got back into the vehicle and left. However, until the truck arrived for the wounded, they forced us to go and remove the mines. I personally removed four or five of them. This was a trip-wire -- these were trip-wire mines, and we would carry the mines, a mine in one hand and the charge in the other. And when I turned around, I saw that there were four rows of clover trampled upon. So it was obvious that the mines had been planted there before. When the trucks arrived, we helped the wounded get on. A local man trod on a small mine, and his toes were blown off. They were loaded onto the truck and taken away. And a young man who was hit in the spine, he kept saying that he had lost a leg, but he had a leg, but obviously it was paralysed. Then they drove them off in the direction of Tovarnik, and they took us back to the village. They told us to go on working as if nothing had happened. When we came to the cooperative, no one was left. There was blood, bloodstains. We dug a trench for the army behind the school. We saw them taking out the Pavic brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we must have a break from the narrative in order that we don't lose it. If we have too much information, it's impossible to take it all in. I don't know if you want to go back and cover any of those details that we've dealt with so far or whether you want the witness to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I do have a few details I'd like to cover, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to when the prisoners were being beaten in the morning when people were being called out supposedly for works, was Mr. Devetak present while these beatings and the stabbing that you described took place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he was present, and this commander of the Valjevci, called Boxer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the clover field to which you were taken, how far is that from the Zadruga building in the centre of Lovas where you were initially held prisoner?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 700 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get from the Zadruga building to the clover field, did you have to pass through a JNA checkpoint, and if so, what happened when your column of men, of guarded men, passed through the JNA checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We had to pass through the main entrance to the village, and when we reached there, they just lifted the obstacle, the ramp, and we passed through, without any problems or questions asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who it was, not by name but by unit or description - name if you have it - who it was that accompanied these prisoners from the Zadruga building to the clover field. Who took you out to the clover field?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The Valjevci. The Valjevci. The men from Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these men from Valjevo, are they also the ones that held the prisoners under guard while you were forced to walk through the clover field? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a JNA vehicle coming by. Was the person in that vehicle a JNA officer or a regular soldier, non-officer?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: He was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where he was, where his vehicle was on the road, was it possible to see the bodies of those people who had been injured or perhaps killed by these mine explosions?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It was possible to see them because the road is about five or six metres higher up than the clover field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where -- were you standing on the road when you said you could look back and see the four rows of mines? Is that where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes. I had to reach the canal, cross the canal, climb up and leave the mines on the edge of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the place where you left the mines, where you turned and you could see clearly where the mines were located, where was that in relationship to where the Valjevci were standing with guns, guarding the prisoners walking through the minefield?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Some were behind our backs, and others were up there on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in a position where they could also see clearly the rows of mines that were in the field?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that the prisoners were asked to march through this minefield, did the soldiers point out to them where these mines were or did they just tell them to walk through the field?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They didn't show us anything. They just said that we had to hold hands and use our feet to trample on the clovers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a boy who was seriously wounded, and then you heard shots and he was killed. Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The young man's name who was wounded died in Tovarnik. His name is Josip Turkalj. And the young man who was killed at the bend of the road, his name was Bosko Bodjanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bodjanac, did you see his body when you were walking back to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes. It was lying on the edge of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of maps and one exhibit. We'll start with the map that is at tab number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Could that be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, do you recognise this as a map of the village of Lovas?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to take one of the red pens that's in front of you there, if you could, please, and could you mark with circles where it was that the tanks were located surrounding the village of Lovas. Just put circles where the tanks were located.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you take a look at the map, there's a road that appears to be going out of Lovas, down towards the lower left-hand corner of the map. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark with an "X" on the map the approximate location of the clover field.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you, by drawing a line through the road that goes back to Lovas, show the approximate location of the JNA checkpoint that you had to go through while you were being marched to the clover field.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Of the 70 men that were originally in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, before we go on, do you want that map exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not in the clip which I have, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the name note for Witness C-1204 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 367 under seal, confidential. The packet of exhibits for Witness C-1204 will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 368. And tab 3 will be additionally marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 368 tab 3.1204.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, of the originally 70 men that were being held in the Zadruga overnight, approximately how many of them were marched to the clover field?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to place before you a document marked in tab 4 of the binder of witness exhibits, which I'd like to have exhibited also. It's entitled Annex I Victims Lovas Minefield, Paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's tab 4 to Exhibit 368.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
