utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us who the people are whose names appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Those are the people who were killed in the minefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the man who was shot on the way to the minefield, does his name also appear on this list; and if so, could you tell us what his name is again.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It is on the list. His name is Bodjanac Bosko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man who was wounded at the minefield but who died later, what is his name and is his name on the list?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, it is. His name is Turkalj Josip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to place one more map in front of you. This is tab 1 of the index binders, which I'd also like to have exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Once we have exhibited -- Mr. McKeon, once we've got the exhibit, just read out the tab numbers. This is Exhibit 368.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I take it you want to do tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at this map and tell us what this map depicts and whether it is an accurate map.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It is correct. It shows the road from our agricultural cooperative, or Zadruga, to the minefield.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't draw this map yourself, is that correct, but it is an accurate map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to have you point out a few locations using this map, and we can use the numbers that are on the map as reference points. Could you tell us, first of all, where on this map is the Zadruga building that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is the clover field that you and the other prisoners were forced to march through?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: It is marked as 9 and 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us on this map the approximate location of the JNA checkpoint that you had to go through on the way to the clover field.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're referring to the place about halfway through the map where it appears there's a road coming in from the left and a road coming in from the right and then two number 6's? Is that where you're pointing to?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it looks like at some point on the map there's a series of lines with dots in the middle, and then there's the ward "kanal" and then it changes from dots on the outside to lines in the middle. What does that represent on this map?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: That represents the point at which they were exchanged with us, on the -- they came in on the outside -- we came in on the outside, and they came inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the map, looking up at 9 and 10 up in the field area, it looks like the four rows of mines are just in the upper part of the field and not the lower part of the field. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And using this map of the field, could you show us the direction of travel of the men who were forced to march through this field.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We first had to go in this direction, and they had to go in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just so our record is clear, when you say "this direction," I believe you pointed from the road on the left side of the map to the edge of the field on the right side of the map. Is that correct? Is that the first route you had to take?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no mines in that part of the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There weren't any mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that first pass through the field, did you then turn direction and go from, on this map, about the middle of the map up to the top and then that's when you went through the minefield?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the soldiers who were holding you prisoner under gunpoint and who started to shoot when the mines first went off, where were they located on this map?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Some of them were at number 10, and the others were on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what happened to the prisoners who were left behind at the Zadruga building and who were not taken to the minefield?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: When we returned, they weren't there any more. All that remained was blood. The next day, we learnt - or I learnt from my friends who went to get them out around the different houses, to pull them out of the basements and the chapel at the church - they had been killed with grenades or bullets, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally given the task at some point to collect -- help collect the bodies of the people that had been killed at the minefield?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The next day, they rounded us up in the morning and took us to the minefield, and that's where we had to collect the bodies of our dead friends and load them up onto a truck. And then they drove the truck off, and it was at the entrance to the village for two days. It was parked there for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What eventually happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They used a dredger to dig a hole, and then they threw in the bodies. That is to say, our people had to -- it was a small hole, so our people had to pile up the bodies one over the other and then fill the hole in with soil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that or where was that hole located where these people were buried?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: At the cemetery, the Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after this incident at the minefields, were any Croatian residents of Lovas forced to leave the village, and if so, what happened to their property after they left?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were forced to leave, and they had to sign a document signing over all their property to SAO Krajina, Western Srem, and Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you eventually leave the village and why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I left on the 24th of December. Round about the 20th of December, the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi, according to what they said, had come back from somewhere where a lot of them had been killed because they came upon an army, some soldiers, and they started taking off people in the evening to basements, and they beat them up there. A Serb came up to me, myself, and warned me that I was on the list for the next day, and he told me if ever I could that I should disappear. I spent that night staying with some relatives, and in the morning, I got a permit from a Hungarian. I went to Sid and then Bijeljina with my family, of course, all of us together. We went to Bijeljina. From Bijeljina, we went on to Tuzla, and then to Zagreb after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibits can come back, I think, for the moment. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a long number so I'm not going to repeat it, Mr. C-1204. Is it true that Lovas was a place where there were no particular problems in the lives of the Serbs, Croats, and Hungarians that lived in it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you first of all mention the events that took place in Borovo Selo, and you talk about that here. You say, on the 2nd of May, 1991 -- and that is common knowledge. Now, I have two questions in that regard: Why are you talking about events only as of that date when you know very well that the events in Lovas took place much earlier? Not the ones that you're testifying about but the ones I'm going to ask you about in connection with all the activities. And secondly, why do you speak about that as the massacre of policemen? Do you know what actually happened in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We watched it on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the police stormed the village and completely, without reason and unselectively, entered the village with several vehicles and started shooting at the homes of the people living there and the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: That's not what I saw on television, nor did I hear it happen that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know about that. You're just talking about what you saw on Zagreb television; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's not go into that. Now, on Zagreb television did you see that there was no JNA in Borovo Selo at all, or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I didn't see those images, but what I did see on television, we didn't see any of those people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that the policemen in Borovo Selo were Chetniks, and according to you, they were people wearing some sort of special caps and insignia, cockades. Were you ever in contact with people of that type, especially in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you say that, then?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We watched it on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You watched it on television. Fine. You then say that you had organised guards, and you speak about that in paragraph 8 of page 2 of your statement. Who decided to set up the guard system, guards and watches?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The council in the village; the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then you said that you had Kalashnikovs in the village and some hunting rifles. Who did you get the Kalashnikovs from?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from, but there were a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know when the HDZ was formed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in 1990. Right. Now, is it true that Jovo Milas, Gracanac Josip, and Marin Vidic, in April 1990, were called to a meeting of the HDZ in the village of Bogdanovci which was convened by Tomislav Mercep, the main coordinator for the HDZ of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mercep, in his introductory address, informed all those present that he had received instructions, as he said, from the central board of the HDZ of Osijek to form a military organisation within the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You don't know about that. Fine. Now, do you know that at that time, a military service was set up, the task of which was to arm the members of the HDZ and to train them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but I don't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, I heard that there was ZNG, National Guard Corps or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this happened in April 1990?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: What? What do you mean? Which fact are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: April 1990, Milos Jovo and Josip Gracanac and Marin Vidic were called to attend a meeting in the village of Bogdanovci of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine, you don't know. Now, do you know -- do you happen -- does the name Stipan Radar mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Radar, Stipan Radar, who was appointed leader of that service for arming and training.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, no, you say. And do you know happen to know Jovo Milas, Josip Gracanac and Marin Vidic? Do those names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they your villagers?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Two of them are and one is from a neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Two from your village and one from a neighbouring village. When they came back from the meeting, they held a meeting in Milas Jovo's house and decided to implement the decisions of the meeting in Lovas itself. Do you know anything about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I am now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you weren't then?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't take part in those meetings at that time in 1990?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Jovo Milas convened an executive board of the HDZ in the village of Lovas attended by Krizmanic Franjo, Branko Krizmanic, Josip Badnjak, Filip Josic, Ivo Madjarevic, Rendulic Tomislav, and Franjo Mulic? Do you know all these people?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I know the people but I don't know about any meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know that a meeting was held and that these military services were set up and all the others?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't hear that they were formed or that meetings were convened?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know that Ivo Madjarevic was the leader of one of those services?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Markica Gracanac was the leader of the military section?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And do you know that at the meetings of the Executive Board of the HDZ in Lovas, Ivo Madjarevic, Franjo Mulic, Branko Krizmanic informed the participants that they had received a quantity of explosives to be used against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, because I didn't attend any of those meetings. I was not a member and so they didn't invite me to attend the meetings nor did I go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about a decision taken in August 1990, a decision taken in the HDZ premises in Vukovar, in the hall of the workers centre, to launch the establishment of so-called volunteer detachments, units? And I'm talking about August 1990.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that after that, that is to say already at the end of August and beginning of September, an Executive Board meeting was held in Lovas and a volunteer detachment formed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that this volunteer detachment which was formed for the Lovas village area numbered 120 persons? It is impossible that you don't know about a detachment and its forming that numbered 120 men. And this Markica Gracanac was the commander of the unit, the detachment.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, do you at least know that this particular detachment took part in a review of volunteer troops held in the village of Bogdanovci in September 1990?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So so many people are going from your village to attend this ceremony, this review of troops, and you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I wasn't interested, and I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. But I'm sure you do know that when this ceremony in the village of Bogdanovci took place, that there was a review of troops, of volunteers in Lovas, 50 people under arms, like the whole of the HDZ in Lovas. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that this volunteer detachment was transported with a bus belonging to the agricultural factory farm to the Bogdanovci ceremony in September?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know because you weren't interested or you had absolutely no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Quite simply, I wasn't interested in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, you say you weren't interested. Now, do you know the following -- all right, I won't ask you that because you'll probably say you don't know how weapons and equipment were supplied. You know nothing about that, I assume.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you at least know whether they asked you to give contributions for the purchase of weapons, from Hungary, for example?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They never asked you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I wasn't employed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't employed, and so they skipped you over.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. All right. How about the names of Ante Gaja from the village of Nustar? Does that ring a bell? Lisa Mara from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Lovas, do you know who the owner of a coffee bar called Viktorija was, and his name was Josip Ninkovic? Do you know the proprietor of that coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I do know Josip Ninkovic but I didn't know that he was the owner of the coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about their activities? Do you know anything about their activities with Franjo Knezevic, Nikica Maric, Jovan Jovanovic, with their journeys to Hungary? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that Ninkovic was arrested because of that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, I heard some rumours going round but I wasn't interested and I didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in 1990, before any conflicts broke out, before anything happened. It's a major event when somebody's arrested in a village, especially linked to things of this kind.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, I just heard rumours about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just heard rumours about it.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself have a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you at least know that all the members of the Executive Board of the HDZ were armed, that they had the same types of Kalashnikovs, precisely the ones that came from these sources?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look through them. I don't know who had what kind of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everything that I've asked you about in 1990, everything that was going on in 1990, because you start testifying as of May 1991, but you say you know nothing about these prior events, nothing at all, although you were in Lovas throughout.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I wasn't interested. I wasn't interested in politics. I wasn't interested in weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. You weren't interested in politics or weapons. But as an inhabitant of the village, I assume you knew that it was a constitutional duty of the army with respect to illegal weaponry to seize those weapons illegally procured. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why, then, was it necessary to have weapons in Lovas? You yourself say that you weren't afraid of the army because you had no reason to fear the army. It was a largely predominantly Croatian village, so why did you need the weapons and the village guards?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We needed them because after Borovo Selo, people were afraid. We were near the border, and we watched television Zagreb and the programmes that were televised and we were afraid. So if somebody procured an automatic weapon of any kind, they would probably keep it in the house. They didn't carry it around as a kind of baton. They would keep the weapons at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've just explained to us - and you have this on page 2 of your statement - that Lovas was attacked before Tovarnik with a tank that shot several grenades and shells. You don't know what the weapon used to fire was. Are you sure it was a tank?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes, it was, because I was between the tanks and the village. So I know that the firing came from a tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nobody was killed on the occasion, you say.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the purpose of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Well, later on, we saw that the steeple of the church had been hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the decisions taken in April 1991, when the security service was set up or, rather, the technical service which had up until then been under the HDZ organisation and turned into the security service?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Josip Milas? Is that a name that rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know of any of his activities in connection with what I've just been asking you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I do know that he's a member of the HDZ now, but when he became a member, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you happen to recall, as a decision was made at the time to search the Serbian houses, do you happen to remember whether they searched these homes, these organised, armed members of the HDZ? Did they search the houses of the Lovric, Vorkapic, Tepavac, et cetera, the Serbian houses? That's what happened. And Mijo Kolic, Keser Braco and others were the perpetrators; they conducted the searches?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about that. Well, how big is the village of Lovas? How many inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 1.800 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see; 1.800. Do you at least know the emergency plan that had been put in place, and other measures?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There was no emergency plan of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that Lovas was divided into five regions at the time, commanded by Marko Gracanac? Do you at least know that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that? All right. And the so-called external defence of the village, commanded by Sabljak and others, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that during the negotiations that you yourself mentioned on page 3 of the statement - and you brought them up a moment ago - that the representatives of the JNA exclusively called for the handing over of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know, at least from the media, that the Presidency of Yugoslavia made a decision to disarm all those who unlawfully were in possession of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I wasn't informed about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that over 70 per cent of the villagers, the inhabitants, left Lovas after the army asked them to hand in their weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the army asked the villagers to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: And the women and children fled to Milica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they flee when the army just asked them to give up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Because they heard from people in Tovarnik what had happened to them, what had happened in their village. That's why they fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that on the 10th of September, an attack was launched on the village and that the village was first shelled.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attacked the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The village was attacked by tanks, and then later on the paramilitary units entered the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that upon entering the village after the attack, you found yourself in a cellar and that on the occasion, you saw a local man among those who were asking you to come out. So actually you saw a neighbour of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were men, Serbs, from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a conflict within the village itself, a local conflict.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No. There were no conflicts up to then at all, because the evening before that, we were together in a coffee bar, Dzuro Prodanovic, Radojcic, so that we had no conflict with them at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on that day, there were no conflicts with them, but you saw them. You didn't see any troops or army members.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I saw them entering the village armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I saw them, those Serbs of Lovas, entering and walking around the village under arms and forcing the Croats to go towards the Zadruga or cooperative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, on that day when the attack started, as you say, you didn't see anybody being killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I saw, across the road to my house, a man lying. Later on, we learnt that it was Josip Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But then you didn't see JNA soldiers or officers.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I did not because I did not leave the house or the yard for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you left and saw them, but here on page 4, this is this long paragraph on page 4, and you say that: "On that day, I didn't see anyone being killed, but two or three days later, we learnt that about 20 or 21 men were killed in the village that day." And then you say: "As the soldiers went away ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have copies -- I didn't mean to interrupt Mr. Milosevic, but we have copies of the statement, if it would help the Court to follow along as he's quoting from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it would, yes. If we could have them, please. Also the witness should have a copy too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say: "As they went away, you heard shots from the other side of the village. Later on, I saw them escorting some people to the Zadruga building," and in brackets it says, "Zadruga is a kind of a village farmer's community."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what Mr. Milosevic is talking about is on page 4, second paragraph of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now wish to quote this sentence of yours. Of course, all of this was stated by you, but this one in particular: "As in the village, since I did not see any JNA soldiers or officers and since all those people who entered the village were armed and wearing various kinds of uniforms, some even civilian clothes, I assumed they were some kind of a paramilitary formation. I also saw that Rakic Zeljko wore Chetnik insignia and presumed that there were also Chetniks among them." And then comes the next paragraph, beginning with the sentence: "That evening, JNA tanks entered the village." So when those people were killed and when this was happening, there were no army members in the village, but it was only that evening that they entered, when they heard that there was shooting there, to secure the village and to stop violence. Was that the role of the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They passed through the village in tanks, and they came out of trucks and buses. They entered the school and forced people out of their houses in order to accommodate the troops. There were volunteers among them too, but in the tanks were mostly young men. And the volunteers, they all wore JNA uniforms, those that came by buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who arrived -- or, rather, JNA soldiers who arrived, that's what I'm trying to establish. So they came subsequent to these events when these people were killed.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They arrived in the evening. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means on the evening of the day when these people were killed. And when they were killed, no one from the JNA was present there. That is what I'd like to make quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So your evidence, so we can follow it, is that the first troops in the village were the locals; is that right? And then the JNA came in in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were locals, but other people also whom we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those locals who were armed didn't enter the village, they were there, weren't they? They didn't come there from anywhere. They were simply in the village. They were living in that village; right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were living in the village, but later on they boasted how they had come from Opatovac and how they had captured the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know what they boasted about, but you said that they were locals and that there were no army members when the killings occurred and that the army arrived in the evening.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The army came in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to say, on page 4, that the JNA came and some reservists who asked you to engage in some sort of forced labour, like removing killed animals, dead animals in the village, putting some order. Is that what you call forced labour?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any army member ask you to do that or was it someone else from your local structures that were organised in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know who gave the order, but in any event, we were informed about it mostly by our local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said here that you had a president of the village who was a local, that the commander in the village was also a local, and that you had such a unit there.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: The main person in the village when they entered, and later who took control of everything, was Ljuban Devetak, who used to live in Osijek before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But also this man who tasked you to be the drummer, who would inform the villagers about the things they felt they should be informed about, he was from your village too, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information that you were forced to provide to the villagers, was that signed by someone else or by a local person?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak. He was a local. He didn't live there. His parents were in Lovas. He was born there but he lived in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. He lived in the town, but he came from that village and was living in the nearby town. So he came there. I see. Fine. So all these persons that we have now referred to were your locals, your villagers.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: There were some villagers, but there were some from the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know where they came from. For instance, this Zeljko Rakic, I knew him because we used to work together in Borovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You testified that they beat you. But please give me a very precise answer: Is it true that you were not beaten by members of the army or anyone from outside your village? Did members of the army beat you? When I'm saying "the army," I mean the JNA.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know who was in command of the Valjevci, but they were the ones who beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What insignia were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms. They were armed. They were orderly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have five-cornered stars?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They didn't wear caps. They mostly wore helmets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a soldier without a cap?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say you were taken to the Zadruga, the cooperative building, and the people who guarded you there, who took you to the Zadruga, they too were not members of the JNA, were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were Valjevci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned some paramilitary groups who certainly didn't belong to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, then, we'll accept that you do not know who they belonged to. And they acted violently. One had a nickname Boxer, the other was Nikola, another one was Petronije. Is it true that not one of them was a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know whose members they were. There were White Eagles, and Dusan Silni, and the Jovic men and the Valjevci, but those are not JNA members. Such detachment units do not exist in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move on. I think we can cover quite a lot of ground quite quickly though I have quite a lot of questions. You explained that you heard from this Boxer that you would serve as a human shield, that through you they would check out whether the Croats would open fire, as you put it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this way, two columns were formed, with guards walking alongside.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, could you be a human shield if the guards were with you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They were with us until we left the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went on alone?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No. They went on the inside, and we were on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not a wide column, if I can put it that way. You just described that this was a road on an embankment, some five or six metres above ground level. This is not a densely populated column. They were going with you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We were exposed from the outside. So if anybody were to open fire, they would hit us first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So the guards, those who were going with you, were with you all the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And they were with you also when they forced you to look for mines, as you said.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Only they withdrew behind us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far behind you were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Ten to 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a mine blows up, do you think it's safe ten metres away?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, since a moment ago you described the events, you recounted the event, so let us look at it from a different angle now. An explosion occurred.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, a jeep or - I don't know - Pinzgauer or whatever, comes with a JNA officer, obviously brought there by the explosion to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't think that anything attracted him to come there. But after talking to the Valjevci, he got in and went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm asking you about the things you testified about a moment ago. He asked what was going on, what had happened, and they told him that the Ustashas had planted the mines, and he told them it wasn't the Ustashas, it was us, we had mined the area, and take those men back and take the wounded to the hospital and that he would send a truck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it clear from that, since they are explaining to the JNA officer that the Ustashas had planted the mines, and he said it wasn't the Ustashas but us, that the JNA had nothing to do with your being taken there, nor did they have any contact with the officer in connection with the mine before the explosion occurred when this officer came to intervene?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I think that they both knew very well about the mines. And the officer himself admitted that he had mined the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But if they tell him that the Ustashas had planted the mines, they didn't know that the army had planted the mines.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know what they knew and didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just interpreting the conversation that you described here for us, because it wouldn't be in his interest to say, "We did it," if they hadn't done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you may be interpreting it. The witness can only say what happened. It will be for us, in due course, to interpret it. Do you think you might finish this witness in two or three minutes, or do you want more time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in two or three minutes, but I'll try to do it very quickly. I think I'm very quick in the cross-examination of this witness, bearing in mind the fact that he can't stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We have to adjourn today pretty promptly because there's another case coming in. Mr. McKeon, can this witness stay or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's clear this up: A JNA member appears only once the shooting or, rather, the explosion was heard?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: When the shooting stopped, he appeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. After the shooting, he appeared?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that the first reaction of that JNA member, when he saw what had happened, was to inquire what had happened? And you say that on page 6 in the one but last paragraph. Anyway, that is what is stated in your statement. Was his reaction best proof that he had nothing to do with your being taken to the minefield?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I don't know about his reaction, but I know that no one could leave the village without a pass. We would be given a red pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the village, did you do so with a pass or in the form of a column to do some work?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes. We went past as a column. The army lifted the barrier, and we passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: This was on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were villagers. You're going to do some work. You're passing by, you're going together with these others, and they're letting you by. They're letting you pass. They're not asking you where you're going. What have they got to do with it? Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We weren't going to do work escorted by armed men. Earlier on, we went in smaller groups of two or threes, with two or three of them escorting us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think we've covered this. He explained to the officer that the Ustashas had planted the mines, and the officer then ordered them to take care of the wounded - saying that that was not true - to take them immediately to the hospital and for the rest to be taken back to the village. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we establish that no people from the army were implicated in the things you testified about?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We cannot, because I think the army knew everything that was happening. They must have known about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is your assumption. It is a customary assumption. But judging by the reaction of the officer that you described, it appears different. You mentioned that there's some sort of a document to the effect that Croats were forced to sign over their property to the SAO Krajina. Did you see that document? Did you sign such a document?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I personally didn't sign it because I fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you see such a document?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I talked to people who had to sign it when they were forced out of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you find that a little -- I don't know how to put it -- a rather transparent fabrication. You know that if somebody does something under coercion, it has no legal effect. So what would be the purpose of anyone signing a document under force of arms? Signing of such a document could only have a formal significance. Did someone make that up?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I think no one made it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you believe that such a thing is possible?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I do believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I won't try to convince you of the highly questionable truthfulness of that. I tried to find this in your statement and I failed to, to the effect that Croats in Lovas had to wear white bands around their arms.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is a very major thing. It would be a sign, a discriminating sign, based on ethnicity. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how come you didn't mention such a cardinal -- a fact of cardinal importance in your statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I think it is somewhere in the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please help me find it. If you can find it, there's no need for you to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Milosevic is right. There's no such reference. I read through the statement several times. This paragraph, it is on page 4, second paragraph of the English version, and there's only mention made of the marking of a house, and the houses that were searched and no weapons were found in them, and he was told this by a neighbour of his.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All Croats had to wear white bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if that is what you claim now, and we agreed that this is of crucial importance, how is it that you failed to mention such a crucial fact in your statement if it is true?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: I said that the houses had to be marked with white sheets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but houses that had been examined and searched in a legal action of the seizure of weapons. And they were searching the houses for weapons. And we noted earlier on that you had weapons. Therefore, there's no dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: But only Croatian houses had to have these white markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I assume that the houses that had been searched were marked. Those that were not searched were not marked.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: All the Croatian houses were marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that only Croatian houses were searched and no Serb houses were searched?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Not a single one was touched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this wasn't a sign that it was a Croatian house but that it has been searched and that there were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No. All Croatian houses were marked with those sheets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your statement - and you heard a moment ago a quotation - that this was a mark that the houses had been searched.

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: But they went from one Croatian house to another to search each and every one of them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need two minutes. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, let's clear up what we have just referred to. In your statement you said that Grkovic, a friend of yours from the village with whom you were on good terms, took you aside and told you to stay in the house and to put a white piece of textile on the gate to indicate that it was a Croatian house and that somebody had already inspected it. You were told this by Grkovic, your neighbour from the village, and no one else?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question: You said -- this is on page 3, third paragraph of the English version, and page 3, second paragraph of the B/C/S version: "I should not forget to say that just before the meeting in the village of the previous day, several Croatian policemen came from Ilok, collected the few Kalashnikovs we had and took them to Ilok." So before the search was carried out, the Croatian policemen collected the Kalashnikovs they had distributed earlier on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I just have a very few questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. McKeon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by the accused whether you were aware that before you were asked to turn in all of your weapons, whether you were aware that the Presidency of Yugoslavia had made a decision to disarm all of those who were unlawfully in possession of weapons. My question to you, sir, is about the paramilitaries that came in after the tank fire. Were they all carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the paramilitaries that roamed freely around the village while the JNA was there, were they all carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: All of them had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paramilitaries that accompanied you from the Zadruga out to the clover field, were they all carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: All of them had automatic rifles and pistols attached to their belts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far from the clover field was the JNA checkpoint that you had to pass by?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: About 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked questions about the JNA car that came by after the explosion, and you said that it had come from the village. After the JNA officer asked what was going on and asked about the explosion, did he turn around, go back to the village, or did he continue in the same direction that had he been going?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: He continued where he'd been going, towards the exit to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from the JNA checkpoint, or any JNA soldier, for that matter, other than this man that drove by in his car, come out to the field to see what had caused this explosion about 600 metres away from the JNA checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- after you collected the bodies and had the bodies on the truck and were driving them back to the village, did you have to go through the JNA checkpoint again?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you went -- as you were going through the checkpoint, did you observe any discussions between the people that had taken you out there and the JNA officers, asking you or asking them what all these bodies were that were lying on this truck and what had caused these casualties?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: They didn't ask anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, you were asked by the accused about the locals who took place -- who took part in the searches that took place on the first day. You were asked whether in fact they hadn't left the village, they were there, and you said no, they came from another village. Did the local Serbs leave your village of Lovas at some point before the main JNA attack on the village took place on the 10th of October?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: We didn't see some of them. We hadn't seen some of them a day or two before, and some of them on the night before the attack were in a coffee bar with me, but in the morning they all went off together with the unknown people and with the locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, you referred to some Kalashnikovs, and I think the amici may have covered this as well, but at the time that you were being asked -- your villagers were being asked at the meeting with the JNA to turn in all automatic weapons, at that point, had all of the Kalashnikovs already been turned in, as far as you know, or were there still automatic weapons in the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C-1204
utterances.text: As far as I know, when the officer asked them to be turned in, there were none left in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C-1204, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May we have an exhibit number for the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
